narrative_blocks.title: Act 1: Context & Catalyst — The Three Estates & The Open-Field Village
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Act 1: The Three Estates & Strip Farming
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] In medieval England, over eighty-five percent of the population lived in small, self-contained rural agricultural villages. Medieval thinkers viewed society not as a collection of individuals, but as an ordained divine hierarchy known as the Three Estates: oratores (those who pray—the clergy), bellatores (those who fight—the aristocratic knights and barons), and laboratores (those who work—the peasantry). Each estate had a divinely appointed duty. Peasants were taught by the pulpit that God had created them to toil with their hands to support the Church and the nobility, and that rebelling against their social betters was a mortal sin against God himself.

[1.2] The economic life of the village was governed by the open-field system. Surrounding the village were two or three massive communal fields divided into narrow, unfenced strips. Every peasant family held scattered strips across different fields, ensuring that good and poor soil was shared equitably. Farming followed a strict three-year crop rotation: one field planted in autumn with wheat or rye for bread, the second planted in spring with barley, oats, or peas for ale and pottage, and the third left fallow (empty) so the soil could recover nutrients. Peasants lived in single-room wattle-and-daub cottages with thatched roofs and dirt floors, sharing their smoky living quarters with their pigs and cattle during freezing winter nights.

source.label: Source A
source.title: Source A: The Luttrell Psalter: Peasants Reaping Wheat Under the Reeve’s Direction (c. 1330)
source.text: The illuminated manuscript depicts peasant men and women bent double cutting wheat with curved sickles, while a manorial reeve stands upright holding a staff of authority, directing their work under the burning sun.
source.provenance: The Luttrell Psalter, commissioned by wealthy Lincolnshire landowner Sir Geoffrey Luttrell, c. 1320–1340 (British Library, Add MS 42130).
source.question: What does Source A indicate about the supervision of peasant agricultural labour in medieval England?
source.model_answer: Source A demonstrates that peasant harvest labour was backbreaking physical toil subjected to strict manorial surveillance, with the standing reeve wielding a rod of office to ensure serfs fulfilled their compulsory harvest quotas.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [1.1]–[1.2], explain how the Three Estates doctrine justified inequality in medieval England.
tasks.model_answer: The Three Estates doctrine taught that God deliberately ordered society into three classes: those who pray, those who fight, and those who work. Peasants were told that hard agricultural labour was their divine duty to sustain the Church and nobility, making social mobility or rebellion a sin against God.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 2: Escalation & Conflict — Feudal Dues & Hampshire Manors: Bishop’s Waltham Palace
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Act 2: Feudal Exploitation & Meon Valley Tithes
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] Most peasants were not free men, but villeins (serfs) bound to the land. A villein could not leave the village, marry off a daughter, or sell an ox without purchasing a license from the lord’s manorial court. Furthermore, peasants owed crushing labour services: week-work (two to three days of unpaid labour every week farming the lord’s personal demesne) and boon-work (forced emergency work during harvest time, even when the peasant’s own crops were rotting in torrential rain). When a villein died, the lord claimed the heriot—the family’s best beast—while the parish priest claimed the second-best beast as a mortuary fee, often leaving grieving widows destitute.

[2.2] The Catholic Church extracted wealth just as aggressively as secular barons. Every villager was legally compelled to pay the tithe: one-tenth of all grain sheaves, piglets, fleece, and eggs surrendered annually to the Church. Right here in Hampshire, this exploitation was embodied in Bishop’s Waltham Palace in the Meon Valley. Founded in the 1130s by Henry of Blois, Bishop of Winchester (brother to King Stephen), this palatial residence became one of the grandest palaces in medieval Europe. The Bishop of Winchester was the wealthiest landowner in Hampshire, controlling over fifty manors, including Bishop’s Waltham, Fareham, and Droxford. An immense tithe barn at Waltham received thousands of bushels of grain and livestock from Meon Valley peasants, financing luxurious episcopal banquets, private deer parks, and French tapestries while local serfs survived on coarse barley bread.

source.label: Source B
source.title: Source B: The Pipe Rolls of the Bishopric of Winchester for the Manor of Bishop’s Waltham (c. 1210)
source.text: “Manor of Bishop’s Waltham: Received from the tithes of the parish: 120 quarters of wheat, 80 quarters of barley, 45 lambs, 60 fleeces of wool, and 200 eggs. Paid in court fines by serfs for failing to perform autumn boon-work on the Bishop’s demesne: 4 pounds, 6 shillings. Fined for brewing ale contrary to the assize: 12 shillings.”
source.provenance: Winchester Pipe Roll, Hampshire Record Office, documenting episcopal manorial revenue, 13th century.
source.question: What does Source B reveal about the relationship between the Bishop of Winchester and local Meon Valley peasants?
source.model_answer: Source B shows that the Bishop of Winchester operated as a wealthy, demanding feudal landlord, extracting enormous agricultural tithes and using manorial court fines to punish local peasants who skipped forced labour or breached brewing regulations.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [2.1]–[2.2], explain how Bishop’s Waltham Palace illustrates the economic power of the Church in medieval Hampshire.
tasks.model_answer: Bishop’s Waltham Palace was financed directly through the extraction of tithes (one-tenth of peasant crops and animals) and court fines from local Meon Valley manors. It reveals that medieval bishops were not merely holy men, but fabulously wealthy feudal landlords living in palaces built on the forced labour of serfs.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 3: Primary Sources & Forensic Evidence — The Power of the Pulpit & The Doom Painting
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] Because virtually all peasants were illiterate and church services were chanted in Latin, the Catholic Church controlled the peasant imagination through visual art, drama, and architecture. Every parish church was decorated with vivid, colourful wall paintings illustrating biblical stories and the lives of the saints. But the most terrifying and dominant artwork in every church was the Doom Painting, painted directly above the chancel arch where every parishioner was forced to gaze upon it during Sunday Mass.

[3.2] The Doom depicted the Day of Judgment at the end of the world. At the top sat Christ in Majesty displaying his bleeding wounds. Below him, the Archangel Michael held celestial balance scales, weighing the souls of the dead. To Christ’s right, the righteous were escorted by St Peter into a heavenly fortress made of glittering gold. But to the left, horrific, grinning demons used iron hooks and chains to drag the damned into the gaping, flaming jaws of a monstrous sea serpent—the Hellmouth. Inside the flames, the damned were boiled in cauldrons, flayed alive, and bitten by vipers. Prominently featured among the damned were dishonest millers who cheated peasants of grain, corrupt bailiffs, and rebellious serfs who withheld their tithes.

sources.label: Source C
sources.title: Source C: Parish Church Doom Fresco (c. 12th–13th Century)
sources.text: The fresco shows Christ seated on a rainbow of judgment. Below, grotesque demons with clawed feet and horns use ropes to drag naked souls into the roaring, fire-filled mouth of a leviathan beast. An inscription reads: *“DEPART FROM ME, YE CURSED, INTO EVERLASTING FIRE.”*
sources.provenance: Contemporary medieval parish church wall painting (preserved at St Thomas, Salisbury and Hampshire churches).
sources.question: Why was the Doom painting in Source C such an effective tool of psychological control over illiterate villagers?
sources.model_answer: It was effective because illiterate peasants could not read the Bible, but the horrifying visual depiction of demons dragging sinners into eternal fire conveyed an unforgettable message: obedience to the priest and Church law was the only way to escape eternal agony.

sources.label: Source D
sources.title: Source D: A 13th-Century Parish Sermon on Paying Tithes and Obeying the Lord
sources.text: “Beware, O Christian soul! If you steal even a single sheaf of barley from Holy Church, or grumble against the tithe due to your bishop, know of a certainty that the devils are stoking a cauldron of molten lead in Hell for your flesh. Serve your earthly lord in humility, for your station was appointed by God, and everlasting joy shall be your reward in paradise.”
sources.provenance: Medieval preacher’s manual (Exempla) used by parish priests to instruct rural congregations, c. 1260.
sources.question: How does the preacher in Source D use religion to reinforce both religious and secular authority?
sources.model_answer: The preacher connects withholding tithes directly to eternal torture in Hell, and commands serfs to obey their earthly lords in humility because God ordained their lower social status, thereby using fear of damnation to prevent social rebellion.

tasks.prompt: Using Sources C and D, explain how the Church ensured peasants paid their tithes without needing an army of tax collectors.
tasks.model_answer: The Church did not need an army because it weaponized psychological terror. As Source C and D show, priests convinced illiterate villagers that withholding tithes was a mortal sin that would result in their souls being dragged by demons into the fiery Hellmouth for eternity.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 4: The Historical Verdict & Extended Writing — Oppression or Resilient Community?
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] Historians debate whether medieval peasant life was an unrelentingly miserable tale of exploitation or a resilient, vibrant communal existence. Early economic historians like Michael Postan and G.G. Coulton painted a bleak portrait of the medieval village: peasants lived in filthy hovels, worked from dawn to dusk under the shadow of famine and disease, and were systematically robbed of their wealth by predatory landlords and ecclesiastical palaces like Bishop’s Waltham.

[4.2] In contrast, modern social historians like Christopher Dyer and Barbara Hanawalt argue that peasants were far from helpless victims. They exercised significant local agency through the manorial jury, negotiated labour obligations, brewed illegal ale, and pooled resources to build stone parish churches. The medieval calendar contained over forty saints’ day holy days (*holidays*) featuring village feasts, morris dancing, and wrestling matches. While the Church and manor court held immense power, English villagers created a rich communal culture that survived centuries of feudal pressure.

extended_writing.enquiry: How far did the Catholic Church and the manor court maintain total control over medieval peasants?

structure_strip.prompt: Explain how the lord’s manor court, week-work on the demesne, heriot death duties, and villeinage restricted freedom.
Explain how Church tithes (such as at Bishop’s Waltham Palace) and Doom paintings enforced obedience through fear of Hell.
Evaluate the counter-argument: how did peasants resist, negotiate through manorial juries, and enjoy communal festivals?

milestones.silver: 2 balanced PEEL paragraphs explaining feudal exploitation alongside peasant resistance (14–16 lines).

extended_writing.model_answer:
The Catholic Church and the manorial court maintained formidable physical and psychological control over medieval peasants, though villagers still managed to carve out areas of agency and community life. Physically and economically, the manorial court held near-total jurisdiction over unfree villeins. Bound to the soil, serfs were legally forbidden to leave the manor or marry without paying fines. They were subjected to compulsory ‘week-work’ farming the lord’s demesne, while the hated ‘heriot’ tax seized the family’s best beast upon a breadwinner’s death. The lord controlled the village mill and bakery, forcing peasants to pay steep tolls to grind corn. Disobedience resulted in heavy fines or stocks ordered by the manorial court.

Simultaneously, the Catholic Church exercised profound psychological and fiscal domination. Every peasant was compelled to pay the tithe—surrendering one-tenth of all grain, fleece, and livestock. In Hampshire, this wealth was channelled into magnificent episcopal residences such as Bishop’s Waltham Palace, built by the Bishop of Winchester in the Meon Valley. The bishop extracted thousands of bushels of grain to finance opulent courts, while illiterate serfs lived in single-room wattle hovels. Furthermore, the Church policed peasant morality through terrifying Doom paintings displayed above parish chancel arches. Fearing that demons would drag their souls into the gaping Hellmouth, peasants viewed obedience to their lords and priests as a matter of eternal salvation.

Nevertheless, control was not absolute. Social historians like Christopher Dyer emphasise that peasants exercised genuine agency. Manorial juries were composed of villagers who regularly colluded to protect neighbours, negotiate labour dues, and hide illicit brewing. Moreover, the medieval calendar provided over forty religious holidays featuring communal feasts, ale-drinking, and dancing. Ultimately, while the combined machinery of manorial serfdom and ecclesiastical terror strictly circumscribed peasant lives, villagers demonstrated remarkable collective resilience, ensuring their existence was not defined solely by exploitation.

quiz.question: What percentage of the population in medieval England lived in rural farming communities?
quiz.q: What percentage of the population in medieval England lived in rural farming communities?
quiz.explanation: Over 90% of England's medieval population lived in agrarian rural villages, labouring on manorial estates to produce food. Towns were small and housed only a tiny mercantile and administrative minority.

quiz.question: What was a 'villein' in the feudal system?
quiz.q: What was a 'villein' in the feudal system?
quiz.answer: An unfree peasant tied to the land
quiz.a: An unfree peasant tied to the land
options: A priest in a parish church
An unfree peasant tied to the land
A knight who fought for the king
quiz.explanation: A villein was an unfree peasant bound to the lord's manor, required to perform heavy labor services (week-work and boon-work) on the lord's demesne land. In return, they held small strips of land in the open fields to feed their families.

quiz.question: Which of the following could a villein NOT do without their lord's permission?
quiz.q: Which of the following could a villein NOT do without their lord's permission?
quiz.explanation: Under manorial law, villeins could not leave the estate, marry, educate their sons for the priesthood, or sell livestock without paying a fine and receiving the lord's explicit consent. They lacked freedom of movement.

quiz.question: What kind of houses did villeins typically live in?
quiz.q: What kind of houses did villeins typically live in?
quiz.explanation: Peasant dwellings were simple single-room huts constructed from timber frames, woven hazel branches (wattle), and daubed with mud, clay, and animal dung. A central open hearth vented smoke through a thatch roof.

quiz.question: Why did peasants often share their huts with animals in the winter?
quiz.q: Why did peasants often share their huts with animals in the winter?
quiz.explanation: During freezing winter months, peasant families brought their oxen, pigs, and sheep inside the hut behind a low partition. The shared body heat of the livestock was essential to keep the family from freezing to death.

quiz.question: What dictated the daily lives and labor of medieval peasants?
quiz.q: What dictated the daily lives and labor of medieval peasants?
quiz.explanation: Peasant life was entirely governed by the agricultural calendar and daylight hours, moving from plowing and sowing in spring to weeding in summer and harvesting in autumn. Harsh winters were spent threshing grain and repairing tools.

quiz.question: What was the most crucial task for a peasant in late summer?
quiz.q: What was the most crucial task for a peasant in late summer?
quiz.explanation: The late summer harvest (August–September) was the most critical moment of the year, requiring every man, woman, and child to gather wheat, rye, and barley before autumn rains rotted the crops. A ruined harvest meant famine.

quiz.question: What was the 'tithe'?
quiz.q: What was the 'tithe'?
quiz.answer: A tax requiring 1/10th of a peasant's produce to go to the Church
quiz.a: A tax requiring 1/10th of a peasant's produce to go to the Church
options: A fee paid to the lord to grind wheat
A tax requiring 1/10th of a peasant's produce to go to the Church
A tax paid directly to the King
A fine for leaving the village
quiz.explanation: The tithe was a mandatory ecclesiastical tax requiring every parishioner to surrender one-tenth of their annual agricultural produce, wool, and livestock to the parish church. The grain was stored in massive manorial tithe barns.

quiz.question: Who controlled the minds and spiritual lives of the peasants?
quiz.q: Who controlled the minds and spiritual lives of the peasants?
quiz.explanation: The Roman Catholic Church exerted total control over medieval spiritual life, worldview, and moral behavior. The Church was the sole authority explaining the universe, salvation, sin, and the afterlife.

quiz.question: Why did almost no peasant refuse to pay the tithe, even during famines?
quiz.q: Why did almost no peasant refuse to pay the tithe, even during famines?
quiz.answer: They feared eternal damnation in Hell
quiz.a: They feared eternal damnation in Hell
options: They had plenty of extra food
They feared eternal damnation in Hell
The King’s army would attack them
quiz.explanation: Peasants paid tithes religiously because they genuinely believed that refusing to support the Church would doom their souls to eternal torment in Hell. Priests warned that crop failures and illnesses were God's punishment for withholding tithes.

quiz.question: What was a Doom Painting?
quiz.q: What was a Doom Painting?
quiz.answer: A giant mural painted in churches depicting the Day of Judgement
quiz.a: A giant mural painted in churches depicting the Day of Judgement
options: A giant mural painted in churches depicting the Day of Judgement
A painting showing how to harvest crops
A portrait of the local priest
A painting of a battle in the local manor house
quiz.explanation: A Doom Painting was a colossal fresco painted directly onto the church wall above the chancel arch, illustrating the Last Judgement. It presented a vivid, terrifying visualization of Christ judging the saved and the damned.

quiz.question: Why did the Church rely on visual art like Doom Paintings?
quiz.q: Why did the Church rely on visual art like Doom Paintings?
quiz.answer: Because the vast majority of peasants were illiterate
quiz.a: Because the vast majority of peasants were illiterate
options: To make the churches look colorful
Because the vast majority of peasants were illiterate
Because the Pope banned written books
quiz.explanation: Because almost all medieval peasants were illiterate and church services were conducted in Latin, the Church relied on visual art, stained glass, and wall paintings to teach scripture. Doom Paintings warned parishioners of the consequences of sin.

quiz.question: According to Doom Paintings, what happened to obedient Christians?
quiz.q: According to Doom Paintings, what happened to obedient Christians?
quiz.answer: They were welcomed into Heaven by angels
quiz.a: They were welcomed into Heaven by angels
options: They were welcomed into Heaven by angels
They were given gold by the priest
They were sent to Purgatory forever
quiz.explanation: In Doom Paintings, righteous and obedient Christians were depicted dressed in white, being escorted by benevolent angels through the golden gates of the Heavenly Jerusalem. Christ sat enthroned on a rainbow above.

quiz.question: How were sinners depicted in Doom Paintings?
quiz.q: How were sinners depicted in Doom Paintings?
quiz.answer: Naked and being dragged by demons into Hell
quiz.a: Naked and being dragged by demons into Hell
options: Naked and being dragged by demons into Hell
quiz.explanation: Sinners were shown naked, bound in iron chains, and being pitchforked by grotesque, fanged demons into the flaming mouth of Hell (the Hellmouth). Among the damned, painters frequently included dishonest millers, alewives, and corrupt bishops.

quiz.question: What was Purgatory in medieval Catholic belief?
quiz.q: What was Purgatory in medieval Catholic belief?
quiz.answer: A place of suffering before Heaven
quiz.a: A place of suffering before Heaven
options: A place of suffering before Heaven
quiz.explanation: Purgatory was believed to be an intermediate spiritual realm where souls destined for Heaven underwent agonizing, purifying fire to atone for unconfessed venial sins. Medieval Catholics believed time in Purgatory could last centuries.

quiz.question: How could a peasant theoretically shorten their time in Purgatory?
quiz.q: How could a peasant theoretically shorten their time in Purgatory?
quiz.answer: By obeying the priest and paying tithes
quiz.a: By obeying the priest and paying tithes
options: By obeying the priest and paying tithes
By refusing to work for the lord
quiz.explanation: The Church taught that peasants could reduce their time in Purgatory by purchasing indulgences, paying for soul-masses, obeying parish priests, and going on pilgrimages to saintly shrines. This generated vast revenue for the Church.

quiz.question: What building was the 'stone heart' of every medieval village?
quiz.q: What building was the 'stone heart' of every medieval village?
quiz.explanation: The parish church was the sole stone structure in most medieval villages, standing as a physical sanctuary and communal hub. In addition to daily Mass, churchyards served as community markets and celebration grounds on saint days.

quiz.question: When did peasants typically slaughter their animals?
quiz.q: When did peasants typically slaughter their animals?
quiz.explanation: Peasants slaughtered most of their cattle and pigs in late autumn (November) because they could not afford to feed them on scarce hay during winter. Meat was heavily salted or smoked to preserve it for winter consumption.

quiz.question: What would happen if the late summer harvest failed?
quiz.q: What would happen if the late summer harvest failed?
options: They would hunt deer in the lord's forest
They would buy food from other countries
The king would send free grain
quiz.explanation: Medieval agriculture had very low yields and virtually no surplus storage from year to year. A single cold, wet summer that destroyed the harvest caused widespread starvation, nutritional diseases, and child mortality across the village.

quiz.question: What material was typically used to build a peasant's hut?
quiz.q: What material was typically used to build a peasant's hut?
quiz.explanation: Peasant huts were built using wattle-and-daub—woven wooden lattices smeared with a paste of wet soil, clay, straw, and cow dung. Floors were beaten earth strewn with reeds and rushes that harbored pests.

vocab.definition: The devastating pandemic of bubonic and pneumonic plague that struck England in 1348, killing an estimated 30–45% of the population.
The lethal bacterium carried by Oriental rat fleas living on black rats, responsible for bubonic plague.
Agonising, blackened inflammatory swellings of the lymph glands in the groin, armpits, and neck, typical of bubonic plague.
The widely held medieval medical belief that infectious disease was transmitted through foul, poisonous air.
A 1351 law passed by Edward III attempting to freeze wages at pre-1348 rates and forbidding peasants from moving between manors.
An economic situation where the sudden shortage of available workers increases their market value and bargaining power.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 1: Context & Catalyst — The Arrival at Melcombe Regis & The Black Terror
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] In June 1348, a merchant vessel from Gascony sailed into the port of Melcombe Regis (modern Weymouth) in Dorset. Aboard the ship were silent, microscopic killers: black rats infested with fleas carrying the deadly bacterium Yersinia pestis. Within days, sailors and port workers collapsed in screaming agony, plagued by burning fevers, vomiting blood, and grotesque, foul-smelling swellings the size of apples in their groins and armpits known as buboes. By August, the plague swept across Hampshire, Southampton, and Winchester, and by November it had engulfed London, killing hundreds of people every day.

[1.2] Medieval medicine was entirely helpless against the pandemic. Physicians believing in Greek humoral theory and miasma (poisonous air) advised lighting aromatic fires of rosemary, sniffing posies of sweet flowers, or bleeding patients with leeches—treatments that only hastened death. The disease appeared in two forms: bubonic plague, spread by flea bites, which killed seventy percent of victims within five days; and the even deadlier pneumonic plague, spread through airborne droplets, which attacked the lungs and killed one hundred percent of victims within forty-eight hours. Across England, parish priests fled their dying flocks, mass burial trenches were dug outside city gates, and church bells tolled day and night. In just eighteen months, between thirty and forty-five percent of England’s population—nearly two million people—perished.

source.label: Source A
source.title: Source A: Henry Knighton, Chronicle of Leicester Abbey on the Black Death (1348–1349)
source.text: “The dreadful pestilence came to Southampton and Bristol, and almost the whole strength of the town perished. There was so great a shortage of priests that many churches were left empty without divine service... Men died so suddenly that in the morning a man was whole and hearty, and by evening he was buried in the churchyard. A huge trench was dug in London wherein bodies were flung in heaps like dung.”
source.provenance: Henry Knighton, Augustinian canon at Leicester, writing contemporary accounts in the 1350s.
source.question: What does Source A reveal about the breakdown of religious and social rituals during the plague?
source.model_answer: Source A reveals that normal Christian burials completely collapsed; priests fled leaving churches empty, and thousands of corpses were dumped into mass communal trenches "like dung" without individual prayers or dignity.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [1.1]–[1.2], describe the physical symptoms and mortality rates of the two forms of the Black Death.
tasks.model_answer: Bubonic plague caused high fevers, vomiting, and agonizing swellings called buboes in the neck, armpits, and groin, killing 70% of victims within five days. Pneumonic plague was an airborne lung infection that caused victims to cough up black blood, killing 100% of sufferers within 48 hours.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 2: Escalation & Conflict — Spiritual Terror & Societal Breakdown
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] In their terror, medieval Englishmen looked to the heavens for explanations. The Church declared that the plague was divine retribution for humanity’s sins—vanity, pride, gluttony, and provocative clothing. Religious hysteria erupted across Europe. In continental towns, bands of Flagellants marched from town to town, stripped to the waist, whipping their bare backs with leather scourges tipped with iron barbs while chanting hymns to appease God’s wrath. In Germany and France, anti-Semitic conspiracy theories falsely accused Jewish communities of poisoning village wells, leading to horrific massacres.

[2.2] In England, the social fabric dissolved. Because the mortality rate among parish clergy was extraordinarily high—approaching fifty percent as faithful priests administered last rites to dying parishioners—the institutional Church suffered a catastrophic loss of prestige and moral authority. In January 1349, Bishop Ralph of Shrewsbury of Bath and Wells issued a desperate emergency decree allowing dying Christians to confess their sins to ordinary laymen, or even women, because no priests could be found. Surviving priests who took over were often young, uneducated, and illiterate, eroding respect for Church hierarchy. Believing the apocalypse had arrived, many citizens abandoned all moral restraint, carousing in taverns and squandering their savings.

source.label: Source B
source.title: Source B: Bishop Ralph of Shrewsbury’s Emergency Letter to the Diocese of Bath and Wells (January 1349)
source.text: “We understand that many people are dying without the sacrament of penance, because priests cannot be found willing to enter the houses of the sick for fear of contagion. Therefore, we instruct you that if anyone is dying and no priest can be had, they should make their confession of sins to any layperson, even to a woman if no man is available.”
source.provenance: Official episcopal register of Ralph of Shrewsbury, Bishop of Bath and Wells, 1349.
source.question: Why was Bishop Ralph’s decree in Source B an astonishing departure from traditional Catholic doctrine?
source.model_answer: It was astonishing because according to strict Catholic doctrine, only an ordained male priest possessed divine authority to hear confession and grant absolution. Permitting confession to laymen and women proved that the plague had pushed the Church to the brink of collapse.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [2.1]–[2.2], explain why the Black Death caused a severe crisis of faith in the Catholic Church.
tasks.model_answer: The Church claimed the plague was God’s punishment, yet prayers, fasting, and holy processions failed to stop it. Furthermore, approximately half of all parish priests died or fled their posts in terror, forcing bishops to allow confessions to ordinary laypeople and shattering the Church’s aura of divine protection.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 3: Primary Sources & Forensic Evidence — Economic Revolution & The Statute of Labourers
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] When the initial terror subsided in 1350, England woke up to an unrecognisable economic landscape. With nearly half the labour force dead, vast swathes of fertile farmland lay unploughed, crops rotted in fields, and unmilked cattle wandered through empty villages. Suddenly, the economic laws of supply and demand swung violently in favour of the working peasant. For centuries, lords had treated serfs as disposable chattel. Now, there was an acute scarcity of labour. Surviving villeins realized that lords were desperate: if the autumn wheat was not harvested, the lord faced total bankruptcy.

[3.2] Surviving peasants took ruthless advantage of the crisis. Villeins refused to perform unpaid feudal week-work and demanded double or triple their pre-plague cash wages, threatening to abandon their manors and seek employment with rival lords who gladly paid high wages in secret. Terrified that the social hierarchy was disintegrating, King Edward III and the baronial Parliament struck back. In 1349, the King issued the Ordinance of Labourers, followed in 1351 by the infamous Statute of Labourers. The law fixed all wages at 1346 levels, made it a criminal offence for a labourer to refuse work, and forbade peasants from leaving their home parishes under penalty of imprisonment or branding on the forehead with the letter ‘F’ for falsity.

sources.label: Source C
sources.title: Source C: The Statute of Labourers, Passed by Parliament (1351)
sources.text: “Because a great part of the people, especially workmen and servants, has now died in this pestilence, many seeing the necessity of masters and the scarcity of servants refuse to serve unless they receive excessive wages... We have ordained that every man and woman in our realm shall be bound to serve for the wages and liveries accustomed in the twentieth year of our reign (1346). If they refuse, they shall be cast into the nearest gaol until they find surety.”
sources.provenance: Official statute enrolled in the Parliamentary Rolls of England, Westminster, 1351.
sources.question: What problem were the King and Parliament attempting to crush in Source C?
sources.model_answer: Parliament was attempting to crush the newfound bargaining power of surviving labourers, who were exploiting the acute labour shortage to demand "excessive wages", by legally freezing wages at pre-plague 1346 levels and threatening imprisonment for disobedience.

sources.label: Source D
sources.title: Source D: Henry Knighton on Peasant Arrogance and Demands (c. 1350)
sources.text: “Workmen were so arrogant and obstinate that they would not listen to the King’s command. If anyone wished to have them, he had to give them whatever pay they demanded: either his crops had to be left unharvested to rot, or he had to give in to the workers’ proud and greedy demands. A reaper who used to earn 2 pence a day now demanded 6 or 8 pence, and meat and good ale besides.”
sources.provenance: Henry Knighton, Augustinian Canon at Leicester, Chronicle, c. 1354.
sources.question: How does Source D illustrate the total failure of the Statute of Labourers in practice?
sources.model_answer: Source D proves the statute was unenforceable because landlords were forced to give in to workers’ wage demands (triple their former pay plus meat and ale) or watch their entire harvest rot in the fields.

tasks.prompt: Using Sources C and D, explain why the feudal system could never return to its pre-1348 state.
tasks.model_answer: Source C shows the desperate, futile attempt by the ruling class to freeze wages and enforce serfdom by law. However, Source D shows that economic reality triumphed over royal decree: landowners had to pay market wages to survive, permanently breaking the feudal grip on peasant labour.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 4: The Historical Verdict & Extended Writing — Did the Black Death Ruin or Liberate?
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] The historical impact of the Black Death has led to fierce debate between demographic pessimists and socio-economic optimists. Traditional historians like Michael Postan emphasized the immense psychological horror, trauma, and physical devastation: entire families were wiped out, village communities vanished, and English culture was haunted by images of the Danse Macabre (Dance of Death) and physical decay for over a century.

[4.2] However, social and economic historians like Christopher Dyer and Rodney Hilton argue that for the surviving lower classes, the Black Death triggered a socio-economic "Golden Age". As land became cheap and plentiful, peasants acquired larger landholdings, exchanged unpaid labour services for cash rents, ate meat and wheat bread instead of gray gruel, and wore woollen dyed cloth. Feudal serfdom received a fatal blow from which it never recovered, laying the long-term foundations for a free wage-earning society. Yet the anger generated by royal wage caps simmered for thirty years, culminating in the explosion of 1381.

extended_writing.enquiry: How significantly did the Black Death of 1348 transform English society and weaken the feudal system?

structure_strip.prompt: Explain the horrific mortality (30–45%), mass plague pits, flight of clergy, and loss of Church authority.

structure_strip.column: 2. Economic Shift & The Death of Feudalism
structure_strip.prompt: Explain how acute labour shortages allowed surviving peasants to demand cash wages, defying the Statute of Labourers (1351).
Weigh the short-term catastrophe against the long-term "Golden Age" for survivors. Did it transform or shatter England?

extended_writing.connectives: The immediate effect of the pestilence was catastrophic because... • In direct consequence, the demographic collapse created... • Economically, this undermined feudalism when... • Although Parliament attempted to resist through the 1351 Statute... • Ultimately, I conclude that...

milestones.bronze: 1 complete PEEL paragraph explaining plague symptoms or labour shortages (8–10 lines).
milestones.silver: 2 balanced PEEL paragraphs explaining demographic horror alongside economic transformation (14–16 lines).
milestones.gold: A full evaluative essay analyzing whether the pandemic triggered a socio-economic "Golden Age" that destroyed serfdom (18–20 lines).

extended_writing.model_answer:
The Black Death of 1348 was the most transformative demographic and economic catastrophe in medieval English history, irrevocably shattering the feudal order and elevating the status of the surviving peasantry. In the short term, the pandemic inflicted apocalyptic destruction. Between June 1348 and the end of 1349, between thirty and forty-five percent of the English population died from bubonic and pneumonic plague. The rapid mortality overwhelmed all medical and religious institutions. Thousands were flung unceremoniously into mass trenches, while up to half of all parish priests perished or abandoned their parishioners. This failure of the Church to halt God’s wrath permanently eroded respect for ecclesiastical hierarchy.

However, in the long term, the Black Death fundamentally transformed English society by destroying the economic foundations of the feudal system. The sudden extinction of nearly two million workers created an unprecedented scarcity of labour. For the first time, surviving villeins held the upper hand over landowning lords: if landowners refused to pay high cash wages, crops rotted in fields. When Edward III and the baronial Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers in 1351 to freeze wages at pre-plague rates and imprison mobile workers, the legislation proved completely unenforceable. Desperate lords paid market wages in secret, and serfs fled manors with impunity.

Ultimately, the Black Death initiated what historians like Christopher Dyer term a socio-economic "Golden Age" for the surviving working classes. Land values plummeted, enabling ambitious peasants to acquire larger consolidated holdings and transition from unpaid feudal bondage to cash tenancy. Diets shifted from coarse barley gruel to meat and white bread. While the catastrophe inflicted unprecedented human grief, it delivered a fatal structural blow to medieval serfdom from which it never recovered.

quiz.question: Which king lost Normandy and Aquitaine to the French?
quiz.q: Which king lost Normandy and Aquitaine to the French?
quiz.explanation: King John (reigned 1199–1216) suffered disastrous military defeats against French King Philip Augustus, losing Normandy, Maine, and Anjou by 1204. These catastrophic losses earned him the derisive nickname 'John Softsword'.

quiz.question: What mocking nickname was given to King John?
quiz.q: What mocking nickname was given to King John?
quiz.explanation: English chroniclers mockingly called King John 'Softsword' due to his military failures on the continent and inability to protect his ancestral lands in France. It contrasted sharply with his brother Richard the Lionheart's military reputation.

quiz.question: Why were the barons angry with King John?
quiz.q: Why were the barons angry with King John?
quiz.answer: He imposed heavy taxes (scutage) and lost wars.
quiz.a: He imposed heavy taxes (scutage) and lost wars.
options: He imposed heavy taxes (scutage) and lost wars.
He gave too much power to the Church.
He refused to go on crusade.
quiz.explanation: The English barons rebelled because John imposed extortionate scutage taxes, abused feudal wardships, and imprisoned noble opponents without fair trials to pay for his wars. His arbitrary financial tyranny pushed the nobility to take up arms.

quiz.question: What document was King John forced to seal in 1215?
quiz.q: What document was King John forced to seal in 1215?
quiz.explanation: On 15 June 1215, the rebel barons forced King John to grant Magna Carta at Runnymede meadow near Windsor Castle. The charter set legal limits on royal prerogative and established that monarchs must rule according to law.

quiz.question: What was the most important principle of Magna Carta?
quiz.q: What was the most important principle of Magna Carta?
quiz.answer: That no one, not even the King, is above the law.
quiz.a: That no one, not even the King, is above the law.
options: That the barons can choose the next king.
That no one, not even the King, is above the law.
That the King must obey the Pope.
quiz.explanation: The enduring significance of Magna Carta was the constitutional principle that the law is supreme over the monarch. It established that even the King is bound by legal rules and cannot govern arbitrarily.

quiz.question: Where was Thomas Becket murdered?
quiz.q: Where was Thomas Becket murdered?
quiz.explanation: Thomas Becket was assassinated inside Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170 by four overzealous knights of Henry II. His death caused a European-wide scandal that forced Henry to abandon his legal campaign against Church courts.

quiz.question: What does 'excommunication' mean?
quiz.q: What does 'excommunication' mean?
quiz.answer: Being officially thrown out of the Catholic Church.
quiz.a: Being officially thrown out of the Catholic Church.
options: Being officially thrown out of the Catholic Church.
Being forced to pay a massive fine.
quiz.explanation: Excommunication was an ecclesiastical sanction that cut off an individual from the Catholic Church, barring them from sacraments, burial in consecrated ground, and church services. For a king, it released subjects from their feudal oaths of obedience.

quiz.question: Who built the first motte and bailey castles in England?
quiz.q: Who built the first motte and bailey castles in England?
quiz.explanation: William the Conqueror introduced motte-and-bailey fortifications to England immediately after landing at Pevensey in September 1066. These earthwork castles could be constructed in a matter of weeks to enforce military dominance.

quiz.question: What was the Harrying of the North?
quiz.q: What was the Harrying of the North?
quiz.answer: William's brutal destruction of crops to stop northern rebellions.
quiz.a: William's brutal destruction of crops to stop northern rebellions.
options: William's brutal destruction of crops to stop northern rebellions.
The invasion of England by the Vikings.
A plague that wiped out the north.
quiz.explanation: The Harrying of the North in the winter of 1069–1070 was William's scorched-earth response to northern rebellions. Norman troops salted fields, burned crops, and slaughtered herds, causing widespread famine that depopulated the region.

quiz.question: What did Henry II want to stop Church courts from doing?
quiz.q: What did Henry II want to stop Church courts from doing?
quiz.answer: Giving lenient punishments to criminous clerks.
quiz.a: Giving lenient punishments to criminous clerks.
options: Giving lenient punishments to criminous clerks.
quiz.explanation: Henry II sought to eliminate 'benefit of clergy', which allowed priests and clerks accused of serious felonies to avoid royal criminal courts. Henry demanded that criminous clerks be tried and punished under the common law of the land.

quiz.question: How did the Black Death originally reach England?
quiz.q: How did the Black Death originally reach England?
quiz.answer: On trading ships arriving at southern ports like Melcombe Regis
quiz.a: On trading ships arriving at southern ports like Melcombe Regis
options: Carried by the invading French army
On trading ships arriving at southern ports like Melcombe Regis
Brought back by crusaders from Jerusalem
quiz.explanation: The Black Death arrived in England in June 1348 via merchant trade ships docking at the Dorset port of Melcombe Regis (Weymouth). Carried by black rats and fleas on board ship grain, the epidemic spread rapidly along trade routes to London.

quiz.question: What is a 'bubo'?
quiz.q: What is a 'bubo'?
quiz.answer: A painfully swollen lymph node, usually in the armpit or groin
quiz.a: A painfully swollen lymph node, usually in the armpit or groin
options: A painfully swollen lymph node, usually in the armpit or groin
A type of plague doctor's mask
A medieval medicine made of herbs
A type of flea that carried the disease
quiz.explanation: A bubo is an agonizingly tender, inflamed lymph node that swells to the size of an apple in the groin, armpit, or neck. It was the hallmark clinical symptom of bubonic plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.

quiz.question: Which of these was a strange cure medieval people attempted to use for the plague?
quiz.q: Which of these was a strange cure medieval people attempted to use for the plague?
quiz.answer: Strapping a live toad or chicken to the buboes
quiz.a: Strapping a live toad or chicken to the buboes
options: Strapping a live toad or chicken to the buboes
quiz.explanation: Desperate medieval healers attempted bizarre folk cures, including strapping plucked live chickens or toads to buboes to 'draw out the venom', or burning aromatic wood. Without knowledge of bacteria, none of these remedies worked.

quiz.question: What is 'miasma'?
quiz.q: What is 'miasma'?
quiz.answer: The medieval belief that bad smells and corrupt air caused disease
quiz.a: The medieval belief that bad smells and corrupt air caused disease
options: A religious prayer to stop the sickness
A type of rat that carried the plague
The medieval belief that bad smells and corrupt air caused disease
quiz.explanation: 'Miasma theory' was the prevailing medieval medical belief that infectious diseases were caused by breathing 'bad air' or noxious vapors arising from rotting organic matter and swamps. Doctors carried sweet-smelling herbs to ward off miasma.

quiz.question: Who were the flagellants?
quiz.q: Who were the flagellants?
quiz.answer: Religious zealots who whipped themselves to earn God's forgiveness and stop the plague
quiz.a: Religious zealots who whipped themselves to earn God's forgiveness and stop the plague
options: Lords who fled the cities to hide in the countryside
Gravediggers who buried the plague victims
Religious zealots who whipped themselves to earn God's forgiveness and stop the plague
Doctors who specialized in cutting open buboes
quiz.explanation: Flagellants were bands of religious zealots who walked through European towns whipping themselves with iron-tipped leather scourges to appease God's wrath. They believed voluntary suffering would earn divine mercy and halt the pestilence.

quiz.question: What economic situation did the massive death toll create in England?
quiz.q: What economic situation did the massive death toll create in England?
options: A complete collapse of all trade
quiz.explanation: Killing between one-third and one-half of the population, the Black Death created an unprecedented national shortage of agricultural laborers. Empty manors and unharvested fields left surviving peasants in an extraordinary position of bargaining power.

quiz.question: Because there were fewer workers after the Black Death, what did the surviving peasants do?
quiz.q: Because there were fewer workers after the Black Death, what did the surviving peasants do?
quiz.answer: They demanded higher wages and better working conditions
quiz.a: They demanded higher wages and better working conditions
options: They voluntarily worked twice as hard for the same pay
They willingly gave their lands to the Church
They demanded higher wages and better working conditions
They refused to farm and all became merchants
quiz.explanation: Recognizing that their labor was desperately needed to prevent harvest collapse, surviving peasants demanded double or triple their pre-plague wages. Many threatened to leave their home manors unless their lords granted freedom and cash wages.

quiz.question: What was the Statute of Labourers (1351)?
quiz.q: What was the Statute of Labourers (1351)?
quiz.answer: A law passed by the government to freeze peasant wages at pre-plague levels
quiz.a: A law passed by the government to freeze peasant wages at pre-plague levels
options: A law guaranteeing peasants the right to strike
A new tax placed only on wealthy merchants
A royal decree granting freedom to all villeins
A law passed by the government to freeze peasant wages at pre-plague levels
quiz.explanation: In 1351, King Edward III's landowner-dominated Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers, ordering that agricultural wages be frozen at 1346 pre-plague rates and penalizing peasants who broke labor contracts. The law caused intense working-class resentment.

quiz.question: How did the Black Death fundamentally weaken the feudal system?
quiz.q: How did the Black Death fundamentally weaken the feudal system?
quiz.answer: Lords had to start paying villeins or risk them running away to rival lords
quiz.a: Lords had to start paying villeins or risk them running away to rival lords
options: Lords had to start paying villeins or risk them running away to rival lords
The Church took over all farming operations
Knights refused to fight in wars anymore
The King lost all his castles to the peasants
quiz.explanation: Faced with labor shortages, feudal lords were forced to commute traditional unpaid labor services into cash wages and let villeins rent land as free tenants. The rigid feudal hierarchy was fatally undermined as peasants gained economic leverage.

quiz.question: Why did many peasants lose faith in the Catholic Church during the Black Death?
quiz.q: Why did many peasants lose faith in the Catholic Church during the Black Death?
quiz.answer: Because priests were dying just like everyone else, and their prayers hadn't stopped the disease
quiz.a: Because priests were dying just like everyone else, and their prayers hadn't stopped the disease
options: Because the Pope ordered them to stop going to church
Because priests were dying just like everyone else, and their prayers hadn't stopped the disease
Because the Church claimed the plague was a blessing
Because the priests ran away to France
quiz.explanation: Because holy prayers and church rituals proved entirely powerless to halt the plague, and thousands of priests abandoned their parishes or died of infection, popular confidence in the clergy was severely shaken. This disillusionment helped spawn early reform movements like the Lollards.

The military commander and chief spokesman of the Kentish rebels who negotiated with King Richard II at Mile End and Smithfield.
A radical hedge priest whose revolutionary egalitarian sermons declared that all men were created equal under God.
The feudal status of being a serf legally bound to an estate and subject to the lord’s arbitrary will.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 1: Context & Catalyst — The Third Poll Tax & John Ball’s Radical Gospel
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] By 1381, tension in the English countryside had reached boiling point. For thirty years following the Black Death, the ruling nobility had used the courts, fines, and the Statute of Labourers to artificially suppress peasant wages and prevent serfs from escaping to free towns. Then came a catastrophic financial blunder. The expensive Hundred Years’ War against France was draining the royal treasury. In 1377, 1379, and 1381, the regency council of the fourteen-year-old King Richard II levied three successive Poll Taxes. The Third Poll Tax of 1381 was brutally regressive: every person over the age of fifteen, rich or poor, had to pay twelve groats (three groats, or one shilling)—equivalent to two weeks’ hard labour for a peasant.

[1.2] Peasants resisted through mass tax evasion: over 400,000 taxpayers vanished from official registers. When royal tax commissioner John Bampton rode into Brentwood, Essex, in May 1381 to extract back-taxes with armed escorts, local fishermen and villagers drove him out with bows and clubs. The revolt spread like wildfire across Essex, Kent, Suffolk, and Norfolk. The rebellion was given moral and philosophical fire by John Ball, an itinerant radical priest who had been repeatedly imprisoned by the Archbishop of Canterbury for heresy. Preaching to thousands on Blackheath, Ball asked the explosive rhetorical question that challenged the entire feudal universe: “When Adam delved [dug] and Eve span [spun], who was then the gentleman?” Ball preached that God had created all men equal, and that the time had come to execute all corrupt lawyers, bishops, and royal advisors.

source.label: Source A
source.title: Source A: Jean Froissart on the Preaching of Radical Priest John Ball (c. 1380s)
source.text: “‘My good people,’ John Ball was accustomed to say, ‘things cannot go well in England, nor ever will, until all property shall be in common, and there shall be neither serf nor gentleman, but we all be equal. How ill they have used us! Why do they hold us in bondage? Are we not all descended from the same parents, Adam and Eve? They are clothed in velvet and warm furs, while we are clothed in poor rags; they have wines and spices and good bread, while we have rye and water.’”
source.provenance: Jean Froissart, French court chronicler, Chronicles of England, France, and Spain (c. 1385).
source.question: How did John Ball use Christian scripture in Source A to attack the feudal hierarchy?
source.model_answer: Ball used the story of Adam and Eve to argue that God created humanity as one equal family without classes, proving that the feudal division between wealthy lords in furs and impoverished serfs in rags was an unnatural, ungodly invention.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [1.1]–[1.2], explain why the Third Poll Tax of 1381 provoked violent rebellion across southeast England.
tasks.model_answer: It provoked rebellion because it was a deeply unfair, regressive flat-rate tax: rich lords and destitute peasants were charged the exact same shilling (equal to two weeks’ peasant wages). Coming after 30 years of post-plague wage suppression, tax commissioners demanding back-taxes sparked violent resistance.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 2: Escalation & Conflict — The March on London & The Fall of the Tower
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] In Kent, the rebels elected Wat Tyler, an articulate and charismatic former soldier, as their supreme military leader. Freeing John Ball from Maidstone prison, Tyler led an army of sixty thousand peasants towards London. On 13 June 1381, sympathetic London apprentices and poor citizens threw open the city gates. The rebels poured across London Bridge. Tyler enforced strict military discipline: looting was punished with death. The rebels were not common thieves; their mission was political retribution. They burned the Savoy Palace, the luxurious mansion of the King’s hated uncle, John of Gaunt, hurling his priceless jewels, tapestries, and silver into the Thames.

[2.2] The rebels also burned the Temple, destroying thousands of court rolls, land registries, and debt bonds that kept them in legal servitude. Fourteen-year-old King Richard II and his terrified royal ministers took refuge inside the formidable stone fortress of the Tower of London. On 14 June, Richard courageously rode out to meet the rebels at Mile End, promising to abolish serfdom, grant land for fourpence an acre, and issue royal pardons. But while Richard was negotiating, Tyler’s men stormed the poorly guarded Tower of London. They dragged out Archbishop Simon Sudbury (the Lord Chancellor) and Sir Robert Hales (the Lord Treasurer), dragged them up to Tower Hill, and hacked off their heads, displaying their severed heads on pikes above London Bridge.

source.label: Source B
source.title: Source B: The Anonimalle Chronicle: The Execution of Archbishop Sudbury (1381)
source.text: “The commons dragged the Archbishop out of the Tower chapel and brought him to Tower Hill. He pleaded with them: ‘Beware, my beloved sons, what you do! If you slay me, the sovereign pastor of your souls, the anger of God will fall upon you.’ But they cried out that he was a traitor to the kingdom and a robber of the commons. Eight blows of an axe were struck before his head was severed from his shoulders.”
source.provenance: The Anonimalle Chronicle, written by a contemporary clerk in the royal administration at York, 1381.
source.question: Why did the rebels target Archbishop Simon Sudbury for execution in Source B?
source.model_answer: The rebels targeted Sudbury not because of his religious office, but because he was the King’s Lord Chancellor who had designed and implemented the hated Poll Tax, making him a symbol of royal corruption and robbery.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [2.1]–[2.2], explain why the rebels burned the Temple and destroyed legal court rolls in London.
tasks.model_answer: The Temple and legal chambers housed the parchment court rolls, manorial registries, and debt contracts that bound peasants to their lords as unfree serfs. By burning these documents, the rebels sought to erase the legal records that enforced feudal bondage.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 3: Primary Sources & Forensic Evidence — The Climax at Smithfield & Royal Deceit
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] On the afternoon of 15 June 1381, the King and the rebels held a second conference in the open horse-market of Smithfield. Wat Tyler rode forward alone on his horse to confront the boy-king, presenting revolutionary demands that went far beyond Mile End: the total abolition of all lordship except the King, the confiscation and division of all Church lands among the people, and the complete equality of all Englishmen. Tensions flared when Tyler rinsed his mouth with water and spat in the dust before the King, and called for a flagon of ale. John Cavendish, a royal esquire, accused Tyler of being a thief.

[3.2] When Tyler drew his dagger, the fiery Lord Mayor of London, William Walworth, drew a short cutlass and slashed Tyler across the neck, while royal esquires ran him through with swords. Seeing their leader fall from his horse, the rebel archers drew their bows, shouting: “Treason! They have killed our captain! Let us shoot!” At that terrifying moment, fourteen-year-old King Richard II spurred his horse directly toward the drawn bows and shouted: “Sirs, will you shoot your king? I am your king and your captain! Follow me into the fields, and you shall have all that you desire!” Mesmerized by the boy-king’s courage, the rebels followed Richard to Clerkenwell Fields, where they were surrounded by freshly assembled royal knights. Tyler was dragged from St Bartholomew’s hospital and beheaded. The disarmed peasants were sent home with empty royal pardons.

sources.label: Source C
sources.title: Source C: The Anonimalle Chronicle on the Murder of Wat Tyler at Smithfield (1381)
sources.text: “The Mayor drew a baselard and struck Wat Tyler on the head, so that he fell sideways upon his horse. Then another squire ran him twice through the body with a sword, and he fell to the ground half dead. When the commons saw it, they cried out: ‘Our captain is slain! Let us slay them all!’ And King Richard gallantly rode forth to them, saying: ‘What work is this, my men? Wat Tyler was a traitor. I am your king; follow me!’”
sources.provenance: Contemporary narrative of the Smithfield confrontation from the Anonimalle Chronicle.
sources.question: How did King Richard II prevent a massacre of the royal party in Source C?
sources.model_answer: Richard showed astonishing presence of mind: by riding straight toward the enraged archers, declaring himself their captain, and promising them everything they desired, he diffused their anger and lured them away from their weapons.

sources.label: Source D
sources.title: Source D: King Richard II’s Revocation of Pardons at Waltham, Essex (July 1381)
sources.text: “When the peasants of Essex came to the King demanding the liberties he had promised under his Great Seal, the King answered them harshly: ‘O you vile wretches, detestable on land and sea! You seek equality with lords? You are not worthy to live. Villeins you were, and villeins you shall remain; in bondage you shall abide, not such as you had before, but incomparably harsher!’”
sources.provenance: Thomas Walsingham, Chronica Majora of St Albans Abbey, recording Richard II’s speech, c. 1390s.
sources.question: What does Source D reveal about the value of royal promises made during the rebellion?
sources.model_answer: Source D reveals that the King’s promises made at Mile End and Smithfield were deliberate, cynical lies. Once military control was re-established, Richard revoked all charters, mocked the peasants as "vile wretches", and vowed to make their servitude harsher than ever.

tasks.prompt: Using Sources C and D, explain how the crown defeated the Peasants’ Revolt through a mixture of bravery and betrayal.
tasks.model_answer: Source C shows Richard II’s personal bravery in riding out alone to calm the armed archers at Smithfield. However, Source D shows that this was followed by absolute betrayal: as soon as royal armies mobilized, Richard tore up his promises and crushed the rebels without mercy.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 4: The Historical Verdict & Extended Writing — Did the Peasants Achieve Anything?
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] In the immediate aftermath of Smithfield, the Peasants’ Revolt appeared to be an unmitigated disaster. King Richard unleashed royal judges and execution squads across southern England, hanging over 1,500 rebels, including John Ball. All charters of manumission were formally revoked by Parliament. Traditional historians viewed the revolt as a heroic but utterly futile explosion of peasant rage that was swiftly crushed by aristocratic force.

[4.2] However, modern revisionist historians argue that the revolt achieved a monumental psychological and political victory. The ruling class had been terrified to its core; for three days, peasants had ruled London and beheaded the Archbishop of Canterbury. Parliament never dared levy another Poll Tax for over six hundred years (until 1989). Furthermore, landowners realized that attempting to enforce unfree serfdom and artificially cap wages was far too dangerous. Over the following century, landlords abandoned forced demesne labour, leased land for cash rents, and permitted serfdom to peacefully wither away. By 1450, English villeinage was effectively dead.

extended_writing.enquiry: Why did the English peasantry rebel in 1381, and to what extent was their rebellion successful?

structure_strip.column: 1. Root Causes & The 1381 Poll Tax Catalyst
structure_strip.prompt: Explain post-plague wage caps, the Statute of Labourers, and the intolerable burden of the Third Poll Tax.
Explain the murder of Tyler at Smithfield, Richard II’s revocation of charters at Waltham, and the execution of 1,500 rebels.

structure_strip.column: 3. Long-Term Significance & The Death of Serfdom
structure_strip.prompt: Evaluate the long-term verdict: poll taxes were abandoned and serfdom withered away. Was it a success in disguise?

extended_writing.connectives: The rebellion was ignited primarily by... • This was exacerbated by thirty years of tension surrounding... • In the short term, the revolt was violently crushed when... • However, in the long term, it proved decisive because... • Ultimately, I conclude that...

milestones.bronze: 1 complete PEEL paragraph explaining the Poll Tax or Wat Tyler at Smithfield (8–10 lines).
milestones.silver: 2 balanced PEEL paragraphs weighing short-term defeat against long-term achievements (14–16 lines).
milestones.gold: A full evaluative essay balancing Richard II’s brutal reaction against the eventual death of English serfdom (18–20 lines).

extended_writing.model_answer:
The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 erupted due to decades of socio-economic frustration, and while it suffered brutal short-term suppression, it achieved profound long-term success in dismantling medieval serfdom. The root cause lay in the aftermath of the Black Death. For thirty years, the baronial elite had used the 1351 Statute of Labourers to artificially freeze wages and block peasant mobility. This combustible atmosphere was detonated by the Third Poll Tax of 1381, a deeply regressive flat-rate tax of one shilling per adult to fund the French war. Combined with John Ball’s egalitarian preaching that all men were created equal under God, the tax sparked open rebellion across Essex and Kent, culminating in the disciplined march on London led by Wat Tyler.

In the immediate short term, the revolt was an unmitigated military failure characterised by royal betrayal. Although the rebels demonstrated immense power by sacking the Savoy Palace and beheading Archbishop Sudbury on Tower Hill, their reliance on the good faith of the monarchy proved fatal. At Smithfield on 15 June, Wat Tyler was murdered by Mayor Walworth, and fourteen-year-old King Richard II deceitfully promised to be the rebels’ captain. Once the dispersed peasant army returned home, Richard mobilized royal armies, revoked all charters of freedom at Waltham, and executed over 1,500 rebels, declaring: “Villeins you were, and villeins you shall remain.”

Nevertheless, in the long term, the revolt fundamentally succeeded in achieving its core objectives. The nobility was shaken to its core by the realization that commoners could seize the capital. Consequently, Parliament abandoned the Poll Tax for over six hundred years, and magistrates ceased rigorous enforcement of the Statute of Labourers. Recognizing that coercive feudal labour risked violent insurrection, landowners voluntarily commuted week-work into cash rents, allowing serfdom to wither away within a century. Ultimately, while Wat Tyler and John Ball perished on the scaffold, their rebellion delivered an irreversible warning to the ruling class, accelerating the birth of a free English working class.

quiz.question: In what year did the Black Death arrive in England?
quiz.q: In what year did the Black Death arrive in England?
quiz.explanation: The Black Death first struck England in the summer of 1348 at Melcombe Regis (Dorset), having originated in Central Asia and swept across Mediterranean trade routes. It decimated English communities over the next eighteen months.

quiz.question: What fraction of the English population was killed by the plague?
quiz.q: What fraction of the English population was killed by the plague?
quiz.explanation: Demographic historians estimate that the Black Death killed roughly one-third to one-half of England's population, reducing it from roughly 4–5 million to under 2.5 million. Entire villages were wiped out or permanently abandoned.

quiz.question: What were 'buboes'?
quiz.q: What were 'buboes'?
quiz.answer: Agonizing, pus-filled swellings caused by the bubonic plague.
quiz.a: Agonizing, pus-filled swellings caused by the bubonic plague.
options: The masks worn to prevent infection.
The fleas that carried the disease.
The doctors who treated the sick.
Agonizing, pus-filled swellings caused by the bubonic plague.
quiz.explanation: Buboes were painful, dark, pus-filled swellings that appeared in the lymph nodes of the groin, neck, and armpits within days of flea bites. If the infection entered the bloodstream (septicemic plague) or lungs (pneumonic plague), death was almost 100% certain.

quiz.question: Why couldn't medieval doctors cure the plague?
quiz.q: Why couldn't medieval doctors cure the plague?
quiz.answer: Because germ theory did not exist yet.
quiz.a: Because germ theory did not exist yet.
options: Because they didn't have enough money.
Because they refused to treat the poor.
Because germ theory did not exist yet.
Because the King banned all medicine.
quiz.explanation: Medieval medicine lacked any knowledge of germ theory or microscopic bacteria, which were not discovered until the 19th century. Doctors relied on ancient Greek humoral theory, bleeding patients and burning herbs to little effect.

quiz.question: What supernatural reason did people blame for the plague?
quiz.q: What supernatural reason did people blame for the plague?
quiz.answer: They believed it was a divine punishment sent by God.
quiz.a: They believed it was a divine punishment sent by God.
options: They believed it was a divine punishment sent by God.
They believed it was caused by comets.
They thought it was a curse from the Vikings.
quiz.explanation: In the deeply religious medieval worldview, the pandemic was universally interpreted as a divine retribution sent by an angry God to punish humanity's sins. Communities organized penitential processions and prayed for divine forgiveness.

quiz.question: What document limited King John's power in 1215?
quiz.q: What document limited King John's power in 1215?
quiz.explanation: Magna Carta was sealed by King John at Runnymede in June 1215 under pressure from armed rebel barons. It established that royal power was subject to law and protected noble liberties from arbitrary monarchical abuse.

quiz.question: Who was murdered by four knights in 1170?
quiz.q: Who was murdered by four knights in 1170?
quiz.explanation: Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170 by four knights after defying King Henry II over the jurisdiction of Church courts. His murder shocked Europe and made his shrine the premier pilgrimage site in England.

quiz.question: Why did King John charge heavy 'scutage' taxes?
quiz.q: Why did King John charge heavy 'scutage' taxes?
quiz.answer: To fund his failed wars to recapture Normandy.
quiz.a: To fund his failed wars to recapture Normandy.
options: To fund his failed wars to recapture Normandy.
quiz.explanation: King John levied eleven scutage taxes in sixteen years to pay for mercenary armies and failed military campaigns in France. This extortionate fiscal pressure was the primary catalyst for the baronial rebellion of 1215.

quiz.question: What was the Domesday Book used for?
quiz.q: What was the Domesday Book used for?
quiz.answer: To record wealth and property for taxation.
quiz.a: To record wealth and property for taxation.
options: To record the laws of the land.
To write the history of the Norman Conquest.
To record wealth and property for taxation.
To list all the knights in the army.
quiz.explanation: The Domesday Book of 1086 was an exhaustive land survey commissioned by William the Conqueror to record the wealth and landholders of England. It enabled the Crown to assess tax yields and feudal obligations with total precision.

quiz.question: Who won the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066?
quiz.q: Who won the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066?
quiz.explanation: King Harold Godwinson won the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066, routing the Viking invasion of Harald Hardrada. However, the victory was followed just weeks later by his fatal defeat at Hastings.

quiz.question: Why was the Poll Tax of 1380 seen as particularly unfair?
quiz.q: Why was the Poll Tax of 1380 seen as particularly unfair?
quiz.answer: It charged every person the exact same amount, meaning it hit the poor much harder than the rich
quiz.a: It charged every person the exact same amount, meaning it hit the poor much harder than the rich
options: It charged every person the exact same amount, meaning it hit the poor much harder than the rich
It required peasants to give up their best farm animals
It only applied to peasants who lived in the north
It was only charged on food and clothing
quiz.explanation: The Poll Tax of 1380 was deeply hated because it levied an identical flat rate of three groats (12 pence) on every person over fifteen, regardless of wealth. This meant impoverished serfs paid the exact same tax as wealthy aristocrats.

quiz.question: Who was John Ball?
quiz.q: Who was John Ball?
quiz.answer: A radical priest who preached that all men were created equal by God
quiz.a: A radical priest who preached that all men were created equal by God
options: A wealthy baron who funded the rebels
A radical priest who preached that all men were created equal by God
quiz.explanation: John Ball was a radical priest who had been repeatedly excommunicated and imprisoned for preaching revolutionary sermons against Church wealth and feudal inequality. He was freed by Kentish rebels from Maidstone prison in June 1381.

'When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?'

quiz.q: How old was King Richard II during the Peasants' Revolt in 1381?
