narrative_blocks.title: Act 1: Context & Catalyst — Henry VI’s Weakness & Bastard Feudalism
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] In 1422, nine-month-old Henry VI inherited two kingdoms—England and France—following the untimely death of his heroic warrior father, Henry V. But as he grew to adulthood, Henry VI proved utterly unfit for the brutal realities of medieval kingship. Pious, gentle, and pathologically naive, Henry hated bloodshed and gave away royal lands and revenues to sycophantic favourites. In 1453, England suffered a catastrophic national humiliation: English armies were routed at the Battle of Castillon, losing all French territories except Calais and ending the Hundred Years’ War. Upon hearing the news, King Henry suffered a catastrophic mental breakdown, sinking into a catatonic stupor for eighteen months, unable to recognise his queen, Margaret of Anjou, or their newborn son.

[1.2] The vacuum of royal authority coincided with a dangerous evolution in the feudal system known as Bastard Feudalism. Under traditional feudalism, knights held land in exchange for military service. Under Bastard Feudalism, wealthy magnates used their vast agricultural revenues to sign cash contracts (indentures) with professional soldiers, providing them with uniforms (livery) and legal protection in local courts (maintenance) in exchange for sworn military service. Powerful "overmighty subjects" like the Duke of Norfolk or the Earl of Warwick commanded private household armies of thousands of archers and men-at-arms. When Henry VI’s government collapsed, Richard, Duke of York, England’s wealthiest magnate and heir presumptive, claimed the Protectorate of the realm. Rival noble families aligned themselves with York (the White Rose) or Lancaster (the Red Rose), transforming personal feuds into national civil war.

source.label: Source A
source.title: Source A: The Crowland Chronicle on the Factionalism and Weakness of Henry VI (c. 1450s)
source.text: “The king was a simple man of peaceful mind, who gave little care to the affairs of state or the defense of his realm, leaving all to his greedy counselors. Meanwhile, the great nobles of the realm maintained armed retinues wearing their badges, so that justice was perverted in every county. No man could obtain his rights unless he wore the livery of an overmighty lord.”
source.provenance: The Crowland Chronicle, written by senior ecclesiastical administrators at Crowland Abbey.
source.question: What dangerous domestic situation under Henry VI is diagnosed in Source A?
source.model_answer: Source A diagnoses the collapse of royal justice caused by a weak, disengaged king, which allowed overmighty nobles with private liveried armies to intimidate courts, pervert the law, and govern shires like autonomous warlords.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [1.1]–[1.2], explain how Bastard Feudalism made civil war far more dangerous in 15th-century England.
tasks.model_answer: Bastard Feudalism allowed wealthy nobles to use cash indentures to build private, permanent armies of professional soldiers wearing their livery. When King Henry VI suffered mental breakdowns and lost control of government, these overmighty subjects used their private armies to fight each other for the crown.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 2: Escalation & Conflict — Towton Bloodbath & The Kingmaker
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] In May 1455, the first blood was shed at the First Battle of St Albans, where Duke Richard of York ambushed the royal court and captured Henry VI. Over the next three decades, the crown was violently seized and swapped six times. In December 1460, Richard of York was killed at Wakefield, his severed head displayed on the walls of York topped with a mocking paper crown. York’s nineteen-year-old son, a brilliant, athletic warrior named Edward, vowed vengeance, claimed the throne as King Edward IV, and marched north to annihilate the Lancastrians.

[2.2] On Palm Sunday, 29 March 1461, fifty thousand men collided in a blinding Yorkshire snowstorm at the Battle of Towton—the largest, longest, and bloodiest battle ever fought on English soil. For ten hours, men fought hand-to-hand in knee-deep snow; Edward IV ordered that no quarter be given. When the Lancastrian lines broke, fleeing soldiers were trapped in the freezing Cock Beck river, where thousands were butchered until bodies bridged the water. Over twenty-eight thousand Englishmen perished in a single afternoon. Edward IV ruled with authority, but his reign was derailed by his greatest ally, Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick ("The Kingmaker"). When Edward refused to be Warwick’s puppet, Warwick switched sides, deposed Edward, and briefly restored the bewildered Henry VI in 1470, before Edward IV returned from Burgundy, killed Warwick at Barnet, and murdered Henry VI inside the Tower of London.

source.label: Source B
source.title: Source B: The Chronicle of the Brut on the Slaughter at the Battle of Towton (1461)
source.text: “On Palm Sunday the two hosts met at Towton in a mighty snowstorm. The fighting was so fierce that the son spared not the father, nor the father the son. The dead lay in piles along the river Cock for six miles, and the snow on the fields was dyed scarlet with blood for weeks afterward. There were slain that day more than eight-and-twenty thousand men, the flower of the chivalry of England.”
source.provenance: The Chronicle of the Brut, contemporary 15th-century English chronicle.
source.question: What does Source B convey about the ferocity and national trauma of the Battle of Towton?
source.model_answer: Source B emphasizes the unnatural brutality of civil war where "the son spared not the father", recording that 28,000 Englishmen died and that blood stained the snow for miles, wiping out the traditional nobility.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [2.1]–[2.2], explain why the Earl of Warwick earned the nickname "The Kingmaker".
tasks.model_answer: Warwick was the wealthiest magnate in England whose immense private armies enabled him to put Edward IV on the throne in 1461. When Edward defied him, Warwick switched allegiances, deposed Edward, and restored Henry VI to the throne in 1470, proving he possessed the military power to make and unmake kings.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 3: Primary Sources & Forensic Evidence — The Princes in the Tower & Bosworth Field
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] When Edward IV died suddenly in April 1483, England plunged into its final, darkest dynastic crisis. Edward left two sons: twelve-year-old King Edward V and nine-year-old Richard of Shrewsbury. Their uncle, Richard, Duke of Gloucester, was named Lord Protector. But Gloucester acted ruthlessly. Intercepting the young king, he lodged the two boys in the royal apartments of the Tower of London for "their safety". He executed their Woodville guardians without trial, declared Edward IV’s marriage invalid due to a pre-contract, declared the boys illegitimate bastards, and crowned himself King Richard III in July 1483. By late summer, the two young princes were never seen alive again. Rumours that Richard had smothered them in their beds horrified the nation and shattered his political support.

[3.2] Opposition coalesced around an unlikely exiled Lancastrian claimant in Brittany: Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond. In August 1485, Henry landed in Pembrokeshire, Wales, with two thousand French mercenaries and gathered Welsh and English supporters. On 22 August 1485, the two armies met at Bosworth Field in Leicestershire. Richard III held numerical superiority, but the powerful Stanley brothers held back their four thousand men on the hillside, waiting to see who would prevail. Desperate to end the battle, Richard spotted Tudor’s royal banner and led an eight-hundred-strong cavalry charge directly across the marsh. Richard cut down Tudor’s standard-bearer and was inches from Tudor when Sir William Stanley intervened, charging into Richard’s flank. Surrounded, unhorsed, and refusing to flee, Richard fought furiously until his helmet was beaten into his skull. Richard’s battered golden crown was retrieved from a hawthorn bush and placed on Henry Tudor’s head as King Henry VII.

sources.label: Source C
sources.title: Source C: Polydore Vergil, Anglica Historia on Richard III’s Final Stand at Bosworth (c. 1500s)
sources.text: “King Richard, seeing his men falling back and Tudor approaching with a small retinue, spurred his horse furiously into the thickest press. He killed William Brandon, the earl’s standard-bearer, and overthrew John Cheney, a man of huge stature. Alone against many, he fought on with indomitable courage, crying out that he would die that day as King of England, until overwhelmed by Stanley’s troops he fell dead in the dirt.”
sources.provenance: Polydore Vergil, Renaissance historian commissioned by Henry VII, writing c. 1506–1513.
sources.question: What impression does Source C give of King Richard III’s death on the battlefield?
sources.model_answer: Source C depicts Richard not as a cowardly villain, but as a warrior fighting with "indomitable courage", slaying Tudor’s bodyguard in personal hand-to-hand combat and choosing to die fighting as King of England rather than fleeing.

sources.label: Source D
sources.title: Source D: The Crowland Chronicle on the Humiliation of Richard III’s Body (August 1485)
sources.text: “King Richard’s body was stripped naked of all clothes, not a rag being left to cover his shame, and tied behind a horse with head and arms hanging on one side and legs on the other, carried into Leicester for all to see. And thus ended the line of the Plantagenet kings, who had ruled England for more than three hundred years.”
sources.provenance: The Crowland Chronicle, contemporary monastic record, August 1485.
sources.question: Why did the victorious Henry VII treat Richard III’s corpse with such deliberate humiliation in Source D?
sources.model_answer: Henry VII needed physical, public proof that Richard III was dead so that no Yorkist pretenders could claim he survived, and parading his stripped body demonstrated to all England that God had chosen Tudor as the rightful sovereign.

tasks.prompt: Using Sources C and D, explain why the Battle of Bosworth Field marked the dramatic conclusion of the medieval Plantagenet dynasty.
tasks.model_answer: Source C shows the last Plantagenet king dying in hand-to-hand combat in the dirt, while Source D shows his corpse being stripped and paraded naked, concluding over three hundred years of Plantagenet rule and paving the way for Henry VII’s Tudor dynasty.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 4: The Historical Verdict & Extended Writing — How Did the Wars of the Roses End?
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] The significance of the Wars of the Roses has been heavily shaped by Tudor propaganda. Shakespeare and Tudor historians portrayed the conflict as an apocalyptic bloodbath that devastated the entire English nation until the providential arrival of Henry Tudor, who united the Red and White Roses by marrying Elizabeth of York. Modern historians have qualified this: the actual fighting occupied fewer than fifteen months across thirty years, ordinary towns and agriculture were largely untouched, and civilian casualties outside battles were minimal.

[4.2] However, for the English aristocracy and the institution of the monarchy, the wars were revolutionary. Sixty noble families were entirely extinguished on the battlefield or the execution block. When Henry VII took power, he clamped down mercilessly on Bastard Feudalism, outlawing private liveried armies and using the Court of Star Chamber to bankrupt disobedient magnates. By centralising royal finance and crushing baronial independence, Henry VII laid the foundations for the powerful, modern Tudor Renaissance state.

extended_writing.model_answer:
The Wars of the Roses tore England apart between 1455 and 1485 due to the toxic combination of a catastrophically weak monarch, the structural disease of Bastard Feudalism, and ruthless dynastic ambition. At the core of the conflict was King Henry VI. Gentle, pious, and prone to catatonic mental breakdowns, Henry was incapable of exercising sovereign authority. His catastrophic loss of all English territories in France by 1453 emptied the royal treasury and filled England with disaffected soldiers. This vacuum of royal leadership was weaponised by Bastard Feudalism: magnates like the Duke of York and the Earl of Warwick signed cash indentures to recruit private armies of liveried retainers, transforming regional rivalries into armed national factions.

Over thirty years, this factionalism escalated into unprecedented dynastic slaughter. The Battle of Towton in 1461 demonstrated the total breakdown of chivalric restraint, leaving twenty-eight thousand Englishmen dead in a single afternoon. The instability was intensified by overmighty subjects like Warwick "the Kingmaker", who deposed monarchs at will. When Edward IV died in 1483, Richard III’s ruthless usurpation and the chilling disappearance of the Princes in the Tower shattered Yorkist political legitimacy, driving moderate nobles to unite behind the exiled Lancastrian claimant, Henry Tudor.

The Battle of Bosworth Field on 22 August 1485 brought a decisive end to the medieval era. When Lord Stanley’s flank attack overwhelmed Richard III’s desperate cavalry charge, the last Plantagenet king died in the mud, extinguishing a three-hundred-year-old dynasty. Henry VII’s accession marked a profound structural transition: by marrying Elizabeth of York, he united the warring factions, while his aggressive legislation banning private liveried retainers crushed the military power of the feudal nobility. Consequently, Bosworth Field ended medieval baronial anarchy and inaugurated the centralized, modern Renaissance state.

quiz.explanation: The Wars of the Roses (1455–1487) was a series of intermittent civil wars fought for control of the English throne between rival cadet branches of the royal House of Plantagenet. The conflict ended the Plantagenet dynasty.

quiz.question: Which two rival branches of the royal family fought in the Wars of the Roses?

options: The House of Tudor and the House of Stuart

The House of Lancaster and the House of York
quiz.explanation: The conflict pitted the House of Lancaster (descendants of John of Gaunt, third son of Edward III) against the House of York (descendants of Lionel of Antwerp and Edmund of Langley). Both houses claimed legitimate hereditary succession.

quiz.question: What flower symbolized the House of Lancaster?
quiz.q: What flower symbolized the House of Lancaster?
quiz.explanation: The red rose of Lancaster became an enduring heraldic symbol of the Lancastrian faction, later popularized by Tudor propaganda and William Shakespeare's historical plays. In reality, Lancastrian kings often used the swan or antelope as badges.

quiz.question: What flower symbolized the House of York?
quiz.q: What flower symbolized the House of York?
quiz.explanation: The white rose of York was the personal heraldic badge adopted by Richard, Duke of York, and his son King Edward IV. It gave the civil conflict its romanticized 19th-century name, 'The Wars of the Roses'.

quiz.question: Why did the Wars of the Roses initially break out?
quiz.q: Why did the Wars of the Roses initially break out?
quiz.answer: King Henry VI was a weak, mentally unstable ruler
quiz.a: King Henry VI was a weak, mentally unstable ruler
options: King Henry VI was a weak, mentally unstable ruler
The King refused to sign the Magna Carta
The peasants revolted against the poll tax
quiz.explanation: The civil wars erupted primarily due to the mental incapacity and political weakness of Lancastrian King Henry VI, who suffered bouts of catatonic mental illness. Powerful nobles exploited his weakness, sparking violent private feuds.

quiz.question: What territory had King Henry VI lost before the Wars of the Roses began?
quiz.q: What territory had King Henry VI lost before the Wars of the Roses began?
quiz.explanation: Under the incompetent rule of Henry VI, England lost virtually all its continental possessions won by Henry V in the Hundred Years' War, retaining only Calais by 1453. Returning defeated soldiers and angry barons destabilized domestic politics.

quiz.question: Who died in 1483, leaving a 12-year-old son to inherit the throne?
quiz.q: Who died in 1483, leaving a 12-year-old son to inherit the throne?
quiz.explanation: The Yorkist King Edward IV died unexpectedly in April 1483 at the age of 40, leaving his 12-year-old son Edward V to inherit the throne under the regency of his uncle, Richard of Gloucester. This sparked a sudden constitutional crisis.

quiz.question: Who was the ambitious uncle of the 12-year-old King Edward V?
quiz.q: Who was the ambitious uncle of the 12-year-old King Edward V?
quiz.explanation: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, was the younger brother of Edward IV and had served loyally as Lord of the North. Upon Edward IV's death, he acted swiftly to seize physical custody of young Edward V from the boy's maternal Woodville relatives.

quiz.question: Where did Richard of Gloucester place his two nephews, supposedly for their own protection?
quiz.q: Where did Richard of Gloucester place his two nephews, supposedly for their own protection?
quiz.explanation: Richard of Gloucester placed 12-year-old Edward V and his younger brother, 9-year-old Richard of Shrewsbury, Duke of York, in royal apartments within the Tower of London, ostensibly to prepare for the coronation. The Tower was both a royal palace and fortress.

quiz.question: What happened to the two young princes after they were placed in the Tower?
quiz.q: What happened to the two young princes after they were placed in the Tower?
quiz.answer: They were never seen in public again

They defeated their uncle in battle
They were never seen in public again
quiz.explanation: By late summer 1483, the two young princes had vanished completely from public view and were never seen alive again. Rumors quickly spread across England and Europe that their uncle had ordered them secretly murdered.

quiz.question: What did Richard III do after declaring his nephews illegitimate?
quiz.q: What did Richard III do after declaring his nephews illegitimate?

quiz.a: He crowned himself King of England

He gave the throne to Henry Tudor
quiz.explanation: In June 1483, Richard declared that Edward IV's marriage to Elizabeth Woodville was invalid due to a pre-contract, rendering the princes illegitimate. Parliament passed the Titulus Regius, and Richard was crowned as King Richard III.

quiz.question: How did the disappearance of the Princes in the Tower affect Richard III?
quiz.q: How did the disappearance of the Princes in the Tower affect Richard III?

It shocked the country and turned many nobles against him

quiz.question: What was the final, decisive battle of the Wars of the Roses?
quiz.q: What was the final, decisive battle of the Wars of the Roses?
quiz.explanation: Fought on 22 August 1485 in Leicestershire, the Battle of Bosworth Field was the climactic engagement of the Wars of the Roses. Henry Tudor's invasion force defeated the royal army of Richard III, founding the Tudor dynasty.

quiz.question: In what year did the Battle of Bosworth take place?
quiz.q: In what year did the Battle of Bosworth take place?
quiz.explanation: The Battle of Bosworth took place on 22 August 1485. It marked the violent overthrow of the Yorkist monarchy and the birth of the early modern Tudor state under King Henry VII.

quiz.question: Who invaded England to challenge Richard III for the throne at Bosworth?
quiz.q: Who invaded England to challenge Richard III for the throne at Bosworth?
quiz.explanation: Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, was an exiled Welsh nobleman with a tenuous Lancastrian claim to the throne through his mother, Margaret Beaufort. He sailed from France with French and Scottish mercenaries to challenge Richard III.

quiz.question: What crucial event happened during the Battle of Bosworth that doomed Richard III?

He was the only king to never wear a crown
He was the first Tudor king
quiz.explanation: Richard III was the last English monarch to die in battle, personally leading a desperate cavalry charge into Henry Tudor's bodyguard before being surrounded and cut down. His lost skeleton was famously rediscovered beneath a Leicester car park in 2012.

quiz.question: Who was crowned King of England after Richard III's death?
quiz.q: Who was crowned King of England after Richard III's death?
quiz.explanation: Following Richard's death on the battlefield, Lord Stanley retrieved the fallen king's crown from a thorn bush and placed it upon Henry Tudor's head, proclaiming him King Henry VII. Henry ruled for 24 years, establishing the Tudor dynasty.

quiz.question: How did Henry VII attempt to heal the division between the rival houses?
quiz.q: How did Henry VII attempt to heal the division between the rival houses?
quiz.answer: He married a princess from the House of York
quiz.a: He married a princess from the House of York
options: He married a princess from the House of York
He moved the capital to York
He banned the use of rose symbols
quiz.explanation: To unite the warring factions, Henry VII married Elizabeth of York, eldest daughter of King Edward IV. He combined the red rose of Lancaster and white rose of York into the iconic Tudor Rose, symbolizing national reconciliation.

quiz.question: What historical period is generally considered to have ended with the Battle of Bosworth?
quiz.q: What historical period is generally considered to have ended with the Battle of Bosworth?
quiz.explanation: Historians generally consider the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485 to mark the transition from the medieval period to the early modern era in England. It ended feudal instability and inaugurated the centralized administrative monarchy of the Tudors.

vocab.definition: A form of government where the monarch holds supreme, unchecked autocratic authority, unrestricted by written laws or parliament.
A system of governance where the monarch’s powers are legally limited and constrained by the rule of law and an assembly.
The doctrine that kings derive their authority directly from God, claiming they cannot be judged by any earthly authority.
Rule by a small, powerful clique of aristocratic noble landowners who dominate or control the crown.
An institutional mechanism, law, or counter-force that prevents an individual ruler from exercising despotic power.
Supreme independent authority and legitimate power over a state and its legal territory.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 1: Context & Catalyst — Royal Power at its Zenith: The Norman & Angevin Kings
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] Across the four centuries between the Norman Conquest in 1066 and the dawn of the Tudors in 1485, the central question of English governance was the boundary of royal authority. On paper, a medieval king appeared virtually all-powerful. By claiming the Divine Right of kings, the monarch was anointed with holy oil at his coronation, placing his person under God’s direct protection. William the Conqueror claimed absolute ownership of every acre of English soil by right of conquest, forcing every baron to swear personal allegiance in the Oath of Salisbury and auditing every hide of land and woodland pig in the Domesday Book of 1086.

[1.2] Under Henry II (1154–1189), royal power expanded through institutional administrative machinery. Henry created the English Common Law, dispatching royal judges on circuits across England and establishing the Court of King’s Bench at Westminster. Through five hundred royal stone castles, mercenary armies, and royal control of taxation, monarchs like William I, Henry II, and Edward I held immense coercive force. Anyone who took up arms against the King committed high treason, punishable by horrific public execution—hanging, drawing, and quartering. To an external observer, the English crown possessed unmatched authority.

source.label: Source A
source.title: Source A: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle Obituary of William the Conqueror (1087)
source.text: “King William was a very wise man, and very powerful, and more worshipful and stronger than any before him. He was mild to good men who loved God, but severe beyond measure to those who resisted his will. If any man wished to live or hold his lands, he must do what the King willed. So harsh was he that no man dared raise a finger against him.”
source.provenance: Contemporary monastic obituary of King William I, The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 1087.
source.question: What impression of royal power does Source A convey regarding William the Conqueror?
source.model_answer: Source A conveys that William held terrifying, near-absolute authority: he was so severe and powerful that no man dared oppose his will, and every landholder’s property and life depended completely upon royal favour.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [1.1]–[1.2], explain how William I and Henry II established the mechanisms of royal power in England.
tasks.model_answer: William I established absolute land ownership through the Domesday Book and feudal oaths, supported by a network of 500 castles. Henry II expanded this by creating the English Common Law and traveling royal judges, centralizing legal power under the crown.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 2: Escalation & Conflict — The Checks on Power: The Church & The Barons
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] In reality, medieval kings were severely constrained by powerful institutional counter-weights. The greatest international limit was the Catholic Church. As the dispute between Henry II and Thomas Becket demonstrated in 1170, the Church operated an autonomous legal system governed by Canon Law, independent of royal sheriffs. When monarchs defied the Pope, Rome wielded devastating spiritual weapons: King John was excommunicated and England was placed under an Interdict in 1208, and Henry II was forced to walk barefoot and be flogged by eighty monks at Canterbury to preserve his crown.

[2.2] Domestically, the King was entirely dependent on his barons. Medieval England had no standing police force or permanent national army; the King could only fight wars, collect taxes, and maintain law and order through the active cooperation of his noble tenants-in-chief. When a king ruled arbitrarily or extorted ruinous taxes, the barons united in armed rebellion. In 1215, the barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta, explicitly subordinating the crown to the rule of law. If a monarch proved hopelessly incompetent or tyrannical, the nobility did not hesitate to depose and murder him: King Edward II was deposed and murdered in 1327, King Richard II was overthrown by Henry Bolingbroke in 1399, and King Henry VI was deposed and murdered in 1471.

source.label: Source B
source.title: Source B: Henry de Bracton, On the Laws and Customs of England (c. 1250s)
source.text: “The King has no equal within his realm. Subjects cannot be the equals of the ruler... But the King himself ought not to be subject to man, but subject to God and to the law, for the law makes the King. Let the King, therefore, bestow upon the law what the law bestows upon him, namely, rule and power. For there is no true king where will rules rather than the law.”
source.provenance: Henry de Bracton, royal judge and chief legal scholar of 13th-century England.
source.question: How does Henry de Bracton define the relationship between the King and the law in Source B?
source.model_answer: Bracton defines the King as subordinate to the law: he asserts that the law creates and empowers the monarch ("the law makes the King"), meaning that if a ruler governs by personal whim rather than the law, he ceases to be a legitimate king.

tasks.prompt: Using paragraphs [2.1]–[2.2], explain why medieval kings could never govern as absolute dictators without baronial consent.
tasks.model_answer: Medieval kings possessed no standing army or police force. They relied entirely on barons to muster knights, collect taxes, and enforce the law in the shires. If a king alienated his barons through arbitrary taxation or tyranny, the barons possessed the collective military power to extract charters like Magna Carta or depose the monarch.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 3: Primary Sources & Forensic Evidence — Economic Upheaval & Dynastic Fragility
narrative_blocks.theme_heading: Act 3: The Threat from Below and Within (1348–1485)
narrative_blocks.text:
[3.1] Beyond the Church and the nobility, royal authority was constrained by economic reality and the common people. The catastrophic demographic shock of the Black Death in 1348 proved that royal decrees were powerless against the laws of supply and demand. When Edward III passed the Statute of Labourers in 1351 to freeze wages, peasants simply ignored the law and demanded market rates. Thirty years later, the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 shook the state to its foundations: armed serfs captured London, stormed the Tower of London, and beheaded the King’s Lord Chancellor, forcing the fourteen-year-old Richard II to plead for his life at Smithfield.

[3.2] Finally, the Wars of the Roses (1455–1485) proved that royal power was only as strong as the individual sitting on the throne. Under the system of Bastard Feudalism, overmighty subjects like the Earl of Warwick maintained private armies that dwarfed the King’s household troops. Between 1461 and 1485, the English crown was seized by force five times. Richard III was hacked to death in the mud at Bosworth Field by rebel nobles, proving that kingship in medieval England was a deeply fragile, highly conditional high-wire act.

sources.label: Source C
sources.title: Source C: John Gower, Vox Clamantis on the Terrifying Power of the 1381 Revolt
sources.text: “The peasant mob rushed like a wild boar, shouting with the voice of devils. They burst through the gates of the capital and took the royal citadel. The King himself trembled behind stone walls, his ministers butchered like sheep before his eyes. Let future kings beware: when the commons arise in wrath, royal majesty counts for nothing.”
sources.provenance: John Gower, contemporary London poet and landowner, Vox Clamantis, c. 1382.
sources.question: What warning does Source C deliver regarding the limits of royal power?
sources.model_answer: Source C warns that when the common people unite in armed rebellion, royal majesty and stone castles cannot protect the King, proving that royal power depends ultimately upon popular stability.

sources.label: Source D
sources.title: Source D: Parliament’s Confirmation of Henry VII’s Title to the Crown (November 1485)
sources.text: “To the pleasure of Almighty God and for the wealth, prosperity, and peace of this realm of England, be it ordained, established, and enacted by authority of this present Parliament that the inheritance of the crown of England... shall remain and abide in the most royal person of our sovereign lord, King Henry the Seventh, and the heirs of his body.”
sources.provenance: Parliament Rolls of Henry VII, First Parliament, Westminster, November 1485.
sources.question: How does Source D demonstrate Parliament’s essential role in legitimising royal power by 1485?
sources.model_answer: Source D shows that even after winning the crown on the battlefield at Bosworth, Henry VII required an act of Parliament to legally enact and validate his royal title, proving that royal legitimacy required parliamentary confirmation.

tasks.prompt: Using Sources C and D, explain how the late medieval period demonstrated that English monarchy was conditional rather than absolute.
tasks.model_answer: Source C shows how peasant uprisings could breach the Tower and threaten the monarch’s life, while Source D shows that even victorious kings required parliamentary acts to confirm their legal sovereignty, proving that power was strictly conditional upon law and consent.

narrative_blocks.title: Act 4: The Historical Verdict & Extended Writing — Absolute or Limited Monarchy?
narrative_blocks.text:
[4.1] In assessing medieval kingship, constitutional historians like William Stubbs and F.W. Maitland argued that medieval England was defined by the gradual, inexorable triumph of the rule of law over royal despotism. From Magna Carta in 1215 to the growth of Parliament under Edward I and Henry VII, English governance established institutional barriers that permanently prevented English kings from ruling as absolute autocrats like their continental counterparts in France or Spain.

[4.2] Conversely, political historians like K.B. McFarlane argue that medieval kingship was fundamentally personal. The constitutional machinery was only as effective as the monarch operating it. A charismatic, ruthless warrior-king like William the Conqueror, Henry II, or Edward IV possessed virtually unchecked power: they taxed their subjects, executed rivals, and waged wars across Europe. However, an incompetent, gentle, or tyrannical king like John, Edward II, or Henry VI faced immediate disaster. Ultimately, medieval monarchy was not absolute: it was a conditional partnership between Crown, Church, and nobility, bounded by the English Common Law.

extended_writing.enquiry: How far do you agree that medieval English monarchs possessed absolute power?

structure_strip.prompt: Explain feudal land ownership, castles, Domesday surveillance, and Common Law under William I and Henry II.
Explain Church autonomy (Becket), Magna Carta (1215), the deposition of tyrannical kings, and the role of Parliament.
Weigh the arguments: was monarchy absolute or conditional? Formulate a sustained, nuanced verdict.

extended_writing.connectives: On the one hand, monarchs appeared to possess absolute power because... • For instance, William the Conqueror demonstrated near-total authority through... • However, in practice, royal sovereignty was severely limited by... • As demonstrated by Magna Carta in 1215... • Furthermore, the Church represented an autonomous power because... • Ultimately, I conclude that...

milestones.bronze: 1 complete PEEL paragraph explaining royal power or checks on the King (8–10 lines).
milestones.silver: 2 balanced PEEL paragraphs weighing royal authority against baronial and Church limits (14–16 lines).
milestones.gold: A full evaluative essay formulating a sustained judgement on personal kingship vs constitutional constraint (18–20 lines).

extended_writing.model_answer:
Between 1066 and 1485, medieval English monarchs possessed immense coercive, legal, and financial authority, but they did not possess absolute power. In theory and under ruthless monarchs, the crown approached absolute dominance. Following Hastings, William the Conqueror claimed total ownership of every acre of English soil by right of conquest, binding his tenants-in-chief through feudal oaths, auditing property in the 1086 Domesday Book, and garrisoning England with five hundred stone and timber castles. Henry II expanded this authority through the creation of English Common Law, circuit judges, and the Court of King’s Bench, centralizing justice under the crown. Furthermore, monarchs claimed Divine Right, anointing themselves with holy oil to place their persons beyond secular reproach. Strong kings could execute rivals for treason, wage aggressive foreign wars, and extract taxation with terrifying efficiency.

However, in practical reality, royal power was strictly conditional and perpetually checked by powerful institutions. The greatest international limit was the Catholic Church. As the martyrdom of Thomas Becket in 1170 proved, the Church was an independent superpower answerable only to the Pope in Rome: Henry II was forced to submit to public physical flogging at Canterbury to salvage his crown. Domestically, kings were entirely dependent on the nobility. Because medieval England had no standing national army or police force, monarchs required baronial consent to raise taxes and govern the shires. When King John abused his prerogatives, the barons seized London and forced him to sign Magna Carta in 1215, legally codifying Clause 39: that no free man could be imprisoned without the lawful judgment of his equals and the rule of law. When monarchs proved hopelessly tyrannical or incompetent, as with Edward II in 1327, Richard II in 1399, and Henry VI in 1471, the barons deposed and murdered them.

Furthermore, the late medieval period proved that royal decrees were powerless against demographic and social realities. The Black Death of 1348 created labour shortages that rendered Edward III’s 1351 Statute of Labourers completely unenforceable, while the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt breached the Tower of London and executed the King’s Lord Chancellor. In the Wars of the Roses, Bastard Feudalism enabled overmighty subjects to depose kings at will, culminating in Richard III’s death at Bosworth in 1485.

Ultimately, I strongly disagree that medieval monarchs possessed absolute power. Medieval English kingship was inherently personal and conditional: while an exceptionally capable, militarily victorious king could exercise near-autocratic command, royal sovereignty was fundamentally an ongoing negotiation. Bounded by Magna Carta, constrained by Church Canon Law, and dependent on baronial cooperation, medieval England was a realm where, as Henry de Bracton famously declared, "the law makes the King."

quiz.question: Which battle in October 1066 established Norman rule over Anglo-Saxon England?
quiz.q: Which battle in October 1066 established Norman rule over Anglo-Saxon England?
quiz.explanation: The Battle of Hastings on 14 October 1066 decisively replaced Anglo-Saxon royal leadership with the Norman dynasty. It began a comprehensive transformation of England's land tenure, architecture, aristocracy, and language.

quiz.question: What type of early wooden castles did William the Conqueror rapidly construct across England to enforce military control?
quiz.q: What type of early wooden castles did William the Conqueror rapidly construct across England to enforce military control?
quiz.explanation: William the Conqueror built over 500 wooden motte-and-bailey fortresses across England to suppress native insurrections and house garrisoned cavalry. Their rapid construction enabled a tiny Norman minority to police a hostile countryside.

quiz.question: What devastating scorched-earth military campaign was carried out in the winter of 1069–1070 by William I to suppress northern rebellions?
quiz.q: What devastating scorched-earth military campaign was carried out in the winter of 1069–1070 by William I to suppress northern rebellions?
quiz.explanation: The Harrying of the North (1069–1070) was William I's systematic campaign of starvation and scorched-earth warfare to crush northern revolts. The resulting devastation depopulated Yorkshire for decades, leaving over 100,000 dead.

quiz.question: What was the hierarchical social and landholding system introduced by the Normans where all land belonged to the Crown?
quiz.q: What was the hierarchical social and landholding system introduced by the Normans where all land belonged to the Crown?
quiz.explanation: The Norman Feudal System established that all land in England belonged directly to the Crown by right of conquest. The King leased land (fiefs) to tenants-in-chief in exchange for military service and financial taxes.

quiz.question: In the Feudal System, what did the King grant to his leading barons (tenants-in-chief) in return for loyalty and military service?
quiz.q: In the Feudal System, what did the King grant to his leading barons (tenants-in-chief) in return for loyalty and military service?
quiz.explanation: In return for immense landed estates (fiefs), tenants-in-chief were bound to provide the King with a specified quota of fully armed, mounted knights for 40 days of annual military duty. They also paid feudal dues and attended the royal court.

quiz.question: What comprehensive survey was commissioned by William I at Christmas 1085 to record wealth and landholding for taxation?
quiz.q: What comprehensive survey was commissioned by William I at Christmas 1085 to record wealth and landholding for taxation?
quiz.explanation: Commissioned at Christmas 1085, the Domesday Book surveyed every landholding in England, detailing tenants, livestock, mills, and annual revenue. It gave William total fiscal oversight of his kingdom and maximized tax collection.

quiz.question: Which Archbishop of Canterbury was assassinated in his cathedral in 1170 after quarreling with King Henry II over the legal power of Church courts?
quiz.q: Which Archbishop of Canterbury was assassinated in his cathedral in 1170 after quarreling with King Henry II over the legal power of Church courts?
quiz.explanation: Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in December 1170 by four knights loyal to Henry II following disputes over Church court privileges. His death made him a global martyr and forced the King to do public penance.

quiz.question: What ultimate religious penalty could the Pope inflict upon a medieval monarch, cutting them off from Church sacraments and releasing subjects from their oaths of loyalty?
quiz.q: What ultimate religious penalty could the Pope inflict upon a medieval monarch, cutting them off from Church sacraments and releasing subjects from their oaths of loyalty?
quiz.explanation: Papal excommunication cut an individual off from all Church sacraments, holy communion, and Christian burial. Applied to a monarch, it released all vassals and subjects from their sacred oaths of feudal fealty, encouraging rebellion.

quiz.question: In what year did rebel barons force King John to attach his seal to Magna Carta at Runnymede?
quiz.q: In what year did rebel barons force King John to attach his seal to Magna Carta at Runnymede?
quiz.explanation: In June 1215, armed rebel barons forced King John to grant Magna Carta at Runnymede meadow near Windsor. The charter established that royal prerogative was subject to customary law and prevented arbitrary monarchical taxation.

quiz.question: What fundamental constitutional principle was established by Clause 39 of Magna Carta?
quiz.q: What fundamental constitutional principle was established by Clause 39 of Magna Carta?
options: The King possessed absolute and divine authority over all courts
No free man could be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land
Peasants were immediately granted freedom from villeinage
Barons were exempt from paying any military taxes forever
quiz.answer: No free man could be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land
quiz.a: No free man could be imprisoned or punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land
quiz.explanation: Clause 39 of Magna Carta established the foundational constitutional principle of habeas corpus and due process of law: no free man could be imprisoned or dispossessed without lawful trial by his peers. It remains in English law today.

quiz.question: Which council of 25 barons created under Clause 61 of Magna Carta marked the earliest ancestor of parliamentary oversight of the monarchy?
quiz.q: Which council of 25 barons created under Clause 61 of Magna Carta marked the earliest ancestor of parliamentary oversight of the monarchy?
quiz.explanation: Clause 61 of Magna Carta, known as the 'Security Clause', created a standing council of 25 barons with the legal right to seize royal castles and lands if the King broke his promises. It was the institutional precursor to parliamentary oversight.

quiz.question: What catastrophic pandemic struck England in 1348, killing approximately one-third to one-half of the population?
quiz.q: What catastrophic pandemic struck England in 1348, killing approximately one-third to one-half of the population?
quiz.explanation: The Black Death struck England in 1348, carried by fleas on black rats arriving on merchant ships from Gascony. It wiped out between 30% and 50% of the entire population within two years, causing a massive societal shock.

quiz.question: How did the Black Death fundamentally alter the economic balance of power between feudal lords and surviving agricultural workers?
quiz.q: How did the Black Death fundamentally alter the economic balance of power between feudal lords and surviving agricultural workers?
options: Lords easily lowered wages and doubled peasant labour duties
The feudal system became strictly permanent with zero social mobility
The acute shortage of labour allowed peasants to demand significantly higher wages and greater freedom
Surviving peasants surrendered all rights to the King
quiz.answer: The acute shortage of labour allowed peasants to demand significantly higher wages and greater freedom
quiz.a: The acute shortage of labour allowed peasants to demand significantly higher wages and greater freedom
quiz.explanation: The acute labor shortage caused by the Black Death inverted the economic balance of power, allowing surviving agricultural peasants to demand significantly higher wages and better terms. Lords were forced to compete for scarce workers.

quiz.question: What restrictive 1351 legislation was passed by King Edward III and the landowning Parliament in an attempt to freeze wages at pre-plague rates?
quiz.q: What restrictive 1351 legislation was passed by King Edward III and the landowning Parliament in an attempt to freeze wages at pre-plague rates?
quiz.explanation: The Statute of Labourers of 1351 was an emergency royal law attempting to freeze wages at 1346 pre-plague levels and punish mobile workers who broke contracts. The law failed in practice and fueled deep peasant resentment.

quiz.question: What hated regressive tax sparked the outbreak of the Peasants' Revolt in Essex and Kent in May–June 1381?
quiz.q: What hated regressive tax sparked the outbreak of the Peasants' Revolt in Essex and Kent in May–June 1381?
quiz.explanation: The Poll Tax of 1380 required every person over fifteen to pay a flat fee of three groats (12 pence) regardless of wealth. This regressive tax fell disproportionately on impoverished rural peasants, sparking the 1381 revolt in Essex and Kent.

quiz.question: Who was the rebel leader who marched on London during the Peasants' Revolt and presented demands to King Richard II at Mile End and Smithfield?
quiz.q: Who was the rebel leader who marched on London during the Peasants' Revolt and presented demands to King Richard II at Mile End and Smithfield?
quiz.explanation: Wat Tyler led thousands of armed Kentish and Essex rebels into London in June 1381, capturing the Tower and presenting demands directly to King Richard II. He was assassinated by the Mayor of London at Smithfield.

quiz.question: Who was the radical priest whose egalitarian preaching ('When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?') inspired the 1381 revolt?
quiz.q: Who was the radical priest whose egalitarian preaching ('When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?') inspired the 1381 revolt?
quiz.explanation: Radical priest John Ball provided the theological justification for the Peasants' Revolt, preaching that social inequality and serfdom were artificial human corruptions absent from God's original creation. He was executed after the revolt failed.

quiz.question: How old was King Richard II when he famously rode out to confront the angry rebels at Smithfield after Wat Tyler was killed?
quiz.q: How old was King Richard II when he famously rode out to confront the angry rebels at Smithfield after Wat Tyler was killed?
quiz.explanation: King Richard II was only 14 years old when he defused the Peasants' Revolt at Smithfield after Wat Tyler was slain. He promised to be the rebels' captain, but later revoked all royal charters of freedom and crushed the rebellion.

quiz.question: What was the long-term impact of the Black Death and the Peasants' Revolt on English feudal serfdom (villeinage)?
quiz.q: What was the long-term impact of the Black Death and the Peasants' Revolt on English feudal serfdom (villeinage)?
options: All English peasants were immediately executed
The monarchy abolished private property entirely
Serfdom steadily disintegrated as landlords found it more profitable to rent land to free tenant farmers for money wages
Serfdom was brutally expanded and lasted until the Victorian era
quiz.answer: Serfdom steadily disintegrated as landlords found it more profitable to rent land to free tenant farmers for money wages
quiz.a: Serfdom steadily disintegrated as landlords found it more profitable to rent land to free tenant farmers for money wages
quiz.explanation: Despite the violent suppression of the 1381 revolt, the economic reality of labor scarcity steadily made serfdom unviable. Over the 15th century, landlords converted labor dues into cash rents, transforming serfs into free wage-earning tenant farmers.

quiz.question: Overall, why is it historically inaccurate to view medieval English monarchs as having 'absolute' power?
quiz.q: Overall, why is it historically inaccurate to view medieval English monarchs as having 'absolute' power?
options: Medieval kings relied constantly on the cooperation of armed barons, the moral and legal authority of the Catholic Church, and the consent of Parliament for taxation
Medieval peasants could vote their kings out of office in annual general elections
Medieval monarchs were strictly figureheads with zero real authority
English monarchs were ruled directly by the King of France
quiz.answer: Medieval kings relied constantly on the cooperation of armed barons, the moral and legal authority of the Catholic Church, and the consent of Parliament for taxation
quiz.a: Medieval kings relied constantly on the cooperation of armed barons, the moral and legal authority of the Catholic Church, and the consent of Parliament for taxation
quiz.explanation: Medieval English kings were never absolute rulers; they were strictly constrained by the feudal baronage's military force, the universal moral and legal jurisdiction of the Catholic Church, and the necessity of parliamentary consent for taxes.

key_individuals.name: William the Conqueror
key_individuals.bio: The Duke of Normandy who launched the Norman Conquest of England in 1066. He defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings, bringing an end to Anglo-Saxon rule and establishing a powerful Norman aristocracy across England.
key_individuals.significance: Fundamentally changed English society, law, language, and landscape, introducing castles and the feudal system.

key_individuals.name: Harold Godwinson
key_individuals.bio: The last crowned Anglo-Saxon king of England. He famously rushed north to defeat the Vikings at Stamford Bridge before marching south to face the Norman invasion at Hastings, where he was killed.
key_individuals.significance: His death marked the permanent end of Anglo-Saxon England and the beginning of Norman rule.

key_individuals.name: Thomas Becket
key_individuals.bio: The Archbishop of Canterbury who fiercely defended the independence of the Church against King Henry II. He was brutally murdered by four knights inside Canterbury Cathedral in 1170.
key_individuals.significance: His martyrdom made Canterbury a major pilgrimage site and forced the King to back down on his religious reforms.

key_individuals.name: King Henry II
key_individuals.bio: A powerful Plantagenet monarch who expanded royal authority across England by developing common law and royal courts. He is also infamous for his disastrous conflict with his former friend, Thomas Becket.
key_individuals.significance: Laid the foundations of the modern English legal system, though his legacy is overshadowed by Becket's murder.

key_individuals.name: King John
key_individuals.bio: One of England's most controversial monarchs. His disastrous military campaigns in France and heavy taxation angered the barons, ultimately forcing him to seal the Magna Carta in 1215.
key_individuals.significance: His failures inadvertently established the principle that the King is subject to the law, not above it.

key_individuals.name: Wat Tyler
key_individuals.bio: The principal leader of the Peasants' Revolt in 1381. He led a massive army of rebels into London to demand an end to the oppressive Poll Tax and the abolition of serfdom.
key_individuals.significance: Though he was killed and the revolt was crushed, his uprising terrified the ruling class and signaled the decline of the feudal system.

key_individuals.name: King Richard III
key_individuals.bio: The last Plantagenet king of England. He seized the throne during the Wars of the Roses and is notoriously associated with the disappearance of the Princes in the Tower.
key_individuals.significance: His defeat and death at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485 marked the end of the Middle Ages in England and the start of the Tudor dynasty.

key_individuals.name: Henry VII
key_individuals.bio: The first Tudor king of England. He won the throne by defeating Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth, effectively ending the chaotic Wars of the Roses.
key_individuals.significance: He restored stability and royal authority, bringing the medieval era to a close and ushering in the early modern period.

guided_reading.book_title: Chronicle of the Kings of England
guided_reading.author: William of Malmesbury
guided_reading.author_context: William of Malmesbury was an English historian writing about 60 years after the Battle of Hastings. In this extract, he describes how the two armies behaved on the night before the battle. As a monk, he had a clear opinion on why God allowed the English to lose.
guided_reading.extract:
"The courageous leaders mutually prepared for battle, each according to his national custom. The English, as we have heard, passed the night without sleep, in drinking and singing, and, in the morning, proceeded without delay towards the enemy; all were on foot, armed with battle-axes... The king himself on foot, stood, with his brother, near the standard; in order that, while all shared equal danger, none might think of retreating.

On the other hand, the Normans passed the whole night in confessing their sins, and received the sacrament in the morning... The infantry, with bows and arrows, formed the vanguard, while their cavalry, divided into wings, were thrown back.

...The English, breathing nothing but blood and treason, resolved to die or conquer. For, as long as they stood firm in a close body, they penetrated every point of the enemy's line."

Glossary
  • Sacrament: A religious ceremony, in this case, taking Holy Communion before facing death.
  • Vanguard: The front part of an advancing army.
  • Treason: The crime of betraying one's country or king (William viewed Harold as a traitor who broke a sacred oath).
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: According to this monk, what were the English doing the night before the battle, and what were the Normans doing?

Pair: Why might a religious writer like William of Malmesbury describe the night before the battle in this specific way? What point is he trying to make about why the Normans won?

Share: Based on this text, what was the greatest strength of the English army, and what was the main difference in how the Normans organized their troops?

guided_reading.book_title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
guided_reading.author: Anonymous Monk
guided_reading.author_context: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle was a year-by-year history of England kept by English monks. When William the Conqueror died in 1087, an anonymous monk who had lived at his court wrote this famous, bitter summary of the king's rule.
guided_reading.extract:
"He caused castles to be built, and oppressed the poor. The king was also of great sternness, and he took from his subjects many marks of gold, and many hundred pounds of silver... He was given to avarice, and greedily loved gain.

He had a great survey made of his kingdom... so very narrowly did he cause the survey to be made, that there was not a single hide nor a rood of land, nor—it is shameful to relate that which he thought no shame to do—was there an ox, or a cow, or a pig passed by, and that was not set down in the accounts...

He made large forests for the deer, and enacted laws therewith, so that whoever killed a hart or a hind should be blinded. As he forbade killing the deer, so also the boars; and he loved the tall stags as if he were their father."

Glossary
  • Avarice: Extreme greed for wealth or material gain.
  • Hide / Rood: Medieval measurements of land.
  • Hart / Hind: An adult male deer (hart) and female deer (hind).
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Pick out the punishment for hunting the King's deer. Write it down.

Pair: The monk writes that it is "shameful to relate" that William counted every single ox, cow, and pig in England. Discuss with your partner: why would an English person in 1086 find the Domesday Book so offensive and shocking?

Share: Look at the phrase: "He loved the tall stags as if he were their father." What does this brilliant piece of sarcasm tell us about William's attitude towards his human subjects compared to his hunting forests?

guided_reading.book_title: Life of St. Thomas
guided_reading.author: Edward Grim
guided_reading.author_context: Edward Grim was a monk who was standing right next to the Archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Becket, when four of King Henry II's knights broke into the cathedral in December 1170. Grim was severely wounded in the attack trying to protect Becket.
guided_reading.extract:
"The wicked knight leapt suddenly upon him, cutting off the top of the crown which the unction of sacred chrism had dedicated to God. Next he received a second blow on the head, but still he stood firm and immovable. At the third blow he fell on his knees and elbows, offering himself a living sacrifice, and saying in a low voice, 'For the name of Jesus and the protection of the Church, I am ready to embrace death.'

But the third knight inflicted a terrible wound as he lay prostrate. By this stroke, the crown of his head was separated from the head in such a way that the blood white with the brain, and the brain no less red from the blood, dyed the floor of the cathedral. The same clerk who had entered with the knights placed his foot on the neck of the holy priest and precious martyr, and, horrible to relate, scattered the brains and blood about the pavements, crying to the others, 'Let us away, knights; this fellow will arise no more.'"

Glossary
  • Unction of sacred chrism: The holy oil used to anoint the heads of priests, making them sacred to God.
  • Prostrate: Lying stretched out on the ground with one's face downwards.
  • Martyr: A person who is killed because of their religious or other beliefs.
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: How does Thomas Becket react to the first two blows of the sword?

Pair: Discuss why Grim includes the gruesome detail of the clerk scattering Becket's brains on the floor and shouting "this fellow will arise no more." What does this tell us about the knights' attitude toward the Church?

Share: King Henry II claimed he never directly ordered the knights to kill Becket. Based on how violently they acted inside a sacred cathedral, do you think they believed they were carrying out the King's true wishes?

guided_reading.book_title: Magna Carta
guided_reading.author: King John and the Barons
guided_reading.author_context: In 1215, King John was forced by his rebellious barons to seal the Magna Carta (The Great Charter) at Runnymede. While much of it was about protecting the wealthy barons' lands, Clauses 39 and 40 became the foundation of modern justice.
guided_reading.extract:
(Clause 39) "No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any way, nor will we proceed with force against him, or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land."

(Clause 40) "To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice."

(Clause 61 - The Security Clause) "The barons shall elect twenty-five of their number to keep, and cause to be observed with all their might, the peace and liberties granted and confirmed to them by this charter... If we, our chief justice, our officials, or any of our servants offend in any respect against any man... those twenty-five barons may distrain upon and assail us in every way possible, with the support of the whole community of the land, by seizing our castles, lands, possessions..."

Glossary
  • Lawful judgment of his equals: The right to a fair trial by a jury of peers, rather than a king just deciding you are guilty.
  • Distrain / Assail: To seize someone's property to force them to do something, and to attack them.
  • Liberties: Freedoms and legal rights.
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Read Clause 40 carefully. What does King John promise he will never "sell," "deny," or "delay" again?

Pair: Look at Clause 61. Discuss what the 25 barons are legally allowed to do if the King breaks the rules of Magna Carta. Why would a medieval King find this clause absolutely humiliating?

Share: Notice the phrase "No free man shall be seized" in Clause 39. Since the vast majority of people in 1215 were unfree peasants (villeins), was Magna Carta really a triumph of liberty for everyone, or just a deal for the rich?

guided_reading.book_title: Aelfric's Colloquy
guided_reading.author: Abbot Aelfric
guided_reading.author_context: Aelfric was an Anglo-Saxon abbot who wrote a textbook (a 'Colloquy') to help boys learn Latin. It features interviews with ordinary workers. Though written just before the Norman Conquest, this famous extract perfectly captures the brutal, unchanging reality of peasant farming that defined the entire medieval period.
guided_reading.extract:
Teacher: What do you say, ploughman? How do you do your work?

Ploughman: O, my lord, I work very hard: I go out at dawn, driving the cattle to the field, and I yoke them to the plough. Be the winter never so stark, I dare not stay at home for fear of my lord; but having yoked my oxen, and fastened the share and coulter to the plough, every day I must plough a full acre or more.

Teacher: Have you any companion?

Ploughman: I have a boy who urges on the oxen with a goad, and he is now hoarse from cold and shouting.

Teacher: What more do you do in the day?

Ploughman: Truly, still I do more. I must fill the oxen's mangers with hay, and water them, and carry out their dung.

Teacher: O, O, it is hard work.

Ploughman: Yes, lord, it is hard work, because I am not free.

Glossary
  • Yoke: A wooden beam used between a pair of oxen to allow them to pull a heavy load.
  • Share and Coulter: The heavy iron blades of a plough that cut into the earth.
  • Goad: A spiked stick used for driving cattle.
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Identify three specific jobs the ploughman must do every single day, regardless of the weather.

Pair: Look at the final sentence: "Yes, lord, it is hard work, because I am not free." Discuss what it actually meant to "not be free" in a medieval village. Why couldn't he just quit and find a new job?

Share: The boy driving the oxen is "hoarse from cold and shouting." Based on this text, what role did children play in the medieval rural economy?

guided_reading.book_title: Knighton's Chronicle
guided_reading.author: Henry Knighton
guided_reading.author_context: Henry Knighton was a monk in Leicester who survived the Black Death. He wrote down what happened when the plague struck England, focusing not just on the horrific human death toll, but on how the sudden lack of workers threw the entire medieval economy into chaos.
guided_reading.extract:
"The dreadful pestilence penetrated the sea coast by Southampton and came to Bristol, and there almost the whole strength of the town died, struck, as it were, by sudden death...

And there died a multitude of sheep and other cattle throughout the country, wandering about without anyone to keep them. They perished in ditches and hedges in unnumbered masses... for there was such a lack of servants and workers that no one knew what to do.

Meanwhile, the King sent word into every shire that mowers and other workmen should take no more than they had before, under the penalties set down in the order... But the workers were so arrogant and obstinate that they did not heed the King’s mandate, but if anyone wanted to have them he had to give them what they asked, and either lose his fruit and crops or satisfy the arrogant and greedy desire of the workmen."

Glossary
  • Pestilence: A fatal epidemic disease.
  • Mandate: An official order or command from the King.
  • Obstinate: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or chosen course of action.
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: According to Knighton, why were the sheep and cattle dying in the ditches?

Pair: Before 1348, peasants had to do what the lords told them for very little reward. Discuss with your partner why the surviving workmen suddenly became "arrogant and obstinate" and demanded higher wages.

Share: King Edward III tried to pass a law forcing peasants to accept the same low wages they got before the plague. Why was this law completely impossible to enforce?

guided_reading.book_title: Chronicles
guided_reading.author: Jean Froissart
guided_reading.author_context: Jean Froissart was a French chronicler who wrote a famous history of the 14th century. Here, he records the revolutionary sermons of John Ball, a radical priest whose ideas fueled the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. John Ball was preaching absolute equality—a terrifying concept to the medieval nobility.
guided_reading.extract:
"A crazy priest in the county of Kent, called John Ball, who for his absurd preaching had been thrice confined in the prison... was accustomed on a Sunday after mass, as the people were coming out of the church, to preach to them in the marketplace and assemble a crowd around him...

'My good friends, things cannot go on well in England, nor ever will until everything shall be in common; when there shall be neither vassal nor lord, and all distinctions levelled; when the lords shall be no more masters than ourselves. How ill they have used us! ...Are we not all descended from the same parents, Adam and Eve? and what can they show, or what reasons give, why they should be more the masters than ourselves?'"

Glossary
  • Vassal: A person in the feudal system who is subordinate to a lord and owes them labor and loyalty.
  • Distinctions levelled: Removing the social classes (rich and poor) so everyone is treated equally.
  • Common: Owned or shared by everyone, rather than privately owned by the rich.
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Froissart calls John Ball a "crazy priest." Find one thing John Ball suggests that would have made a medieval nobleman think he was insane.

Pair: Look at John Ball's use of religion: "Are we not all descended from the same parents, Adam and Eve?" Discuss how he is using the Bible as a weapon against the King and the Lords.

Share: The medieval system (the Feudal System) was based on a strict hierarchy where God placed the King at the top and the peasants at the bottom. How does John Ball's sermon threaten to destroy that entire worldview?

guided_reading.book_title: The Croyland Chronicle
guided_reading.author: Monks of Croyland Abbey
guided_reading.author_context: The Croyland Chronicle was written by monks with deep connections to the royal court. This extract describes the brutal climax of the Wars of the Roses at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485, where King Richard III led a desperate, suicidal cavalry charge directly at Henry Tudor.
guided_reading.extract:
"A fierce and most cruel battle was joined by the vanguards... But when the king [Richard III] saw that in the place where the earl of Richmond [Henry Tudor], his enemy, was standing, there were not many soldiers, he spurred his horse and rode outside his own lines, and made an attack on the earl's position.

The fighting was extremely fierce... and King Richard fell in the field, pierced with numerous deadly wounds, fighting manfully and most valiantly in the thickest press of his enemies.

...The body of the said King Richard was found stripped of all its clothing, and was thrown over a horse, the head and arms hanging down on one side, and the legs on the other; and in this most wretched condition he was carried into Leicester. And the earl of Richmond, receiving the crown from the Lord Stanley, was hailed by the whole army as King Henry the Seventh."

Glossary
  • Vanguard: The leading units advancing into battle.
  • Valiantly: With courage or determination.
  • Wretched: In a very unhappy, unfortunate, or undignified state.
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: According to this chronicle, did King Richard III die running away, or fighting? Note down the exact phrase that proves your answer.

Pair: Discuss the treatment of Richard III's dead body. Why would the victorious Henry Tudor want the dead king to be stripped naked and draped over a horse for everyone in Leicester to see?

Share: At the Battle of Hastings in 1066, King Harold died on the battlefield and the crown was taken by force. In 1485 at Bosworth, Richard III died on the battlefield and the crown was taken by force. After 400 years, had royal power in England really changed at all?

guided_reading.book_title: On the Laws and Customs of England
guided_reading.author: Henry de Bracton
guided_reading.author_context: Henry de Bracton was a judge in the 1250s who wrote a massive book attempting to explain the laws of England. In this famous passage, he wrestles with the ultimate question of the Middle Ages: is the King above the law, or is the King subject to the law?
guided_reading.extract:
"The king has no equal within his realm. Subjects cannot be the equals of the ruler, because he would thereby lose his rule, since equal can have no authority over equal...

But the king himself ought not to be subject to man, but subject to God and to the law, for the law makes the king. Let the king, therefore, bestow upon the law what the law bestows upon him, namely, rule and power. For there is no king where will rules rather than the law."

Glossary
  • Realm: A kingdom.
  • Bestow: To grant or present an honor, right, or gift.
  • Will rules rather than the law: When a king acts purely on his own selfish desires and moods ("will") instead of following established rules.
guided_reading.hinge_question:
Think: Write down Bracton's explanation for why no subject can ever be equal to the King.

Pair: "There is no king where will rules rather than the law." Discuss what this means. According to Bracton, what happens to a King if he ignores the law and just does whatever he wants?

Share: Think back across the whole unit (William the Conqueror, Henry II and Becket, King John and Magna Carta, Richard III). Give an example of a medieval monarch who thought they were above the law, and discuss what happened to them.
